# TalentFlow Q3 Roadmap — Analysis Plan

## Context

This is a 2-hour PM take-home: use Claude Code + the Airtable REST API to turn Acme's
real recruiting-ops data into a defensible Q3 roadmap. The VP of People has made two
claims by email (job boards drive 26.9% of hires and deserve accelerated integration
work; offer acceptance is ~72% and needs to move) and wants 6 engineer-weeks allocated
against them. Five deliverables are scored, D4 (data trust, 30 pts) weighted higher
than D2 (the roadmap itself, 20 pts) — the brief is explicitly rewarding skepticism
over a polished plan.

All 8 tables are already pulled locally (`talentflow/data/*.json`, 892 records) and a
browsable version is published. This plan documents what the data deep-dive already
found and lays out the specific follow-up checks needed before I write the five
deliverables — it does not draft the deliverables themselves yet.

## What the deep-dive already found

**Claim 1 — "job boards bring 26.9% of hires, biggest channel by a wide margin"**
- The number is correct at the application level: of 26 `Hired`-stage applications,
  7 trace to Job Board candidates = 26.9%. But **Referral also produces exactly 7
  hires = 26.9%** — they're tied, not "a wide margin." Job Board only leads on raw
  volume (236 of 350 applications; 191 of 300 candidates).
- Candidate→hire conversion tells the opposite story: Job Board converts 7/191 = 3.7%.
  Referral converts 5/8 = 62.5% (candidate-level; some candidates have 2 applications,
  which is why app-level and candidate-level hire counts differ slightly — 26 vs 24).
  Agency 11.4%, Career Site 16.1%, LinkedIn 9.7%, Campus 0/4.
- Reading: job boards win on volume, not efficiency. "Bring forward the integration"
  is arguable but the VP's own framing ("wide margin") doesn't survive contact with
  the data — this needs to be said plainly in D1.

**Claim 2 — "offer acceptance rate is ~72%"**
- 36 offers total: 26 Accepted, 5 Declined, 5 Pending. 26/36 = 72.2% — matches the VP
  exactly, but only if Pending offers are counted as failures in the denominator.
- Exclude Pending (treat as still-undecided): 26/31 = 83.9%. An 11.7-point swing on
  one definitional choice — this is the crux of D3.
- The 5 "Pending" offers are 20 to **222 days old** (as of the latest data ~2026-08-27).
  A 7-month-old "pending" offer is not a live decision in progress, it's abandoned and
  never closed out. Treating it as genuinely pending (and excluding it) inflates the
  acceptance rate; treating it as a failure (72.2%) is closer to true but conflates
  "candidate said no" with "nobody ever closed the loop." Neither raw number is fully
  trustworthy without a staleness rule — this is what D3 needs to fix.

**Data-quality issues found so far (candidates for D4, with materiality)**
- 6 pairs of candidate records (12 of 300 = 4%) share identical phone + full name but
  different email and Candidate ID — near-certain duplicate people, likely re-applying
  under a different email. This directly risks inflating Job Board's application/
  candidate counts and understating true per-channel conversion (need to re-run Claim 1
  after collapsing these).
- 4 Application IDs (APP-00001, 00005, 00007, 00010) are each reused across two
  completely different application records (different candidates, openings, stages).
  `Application ID` is not a safe join key — anything downstream that joins on it
  instead of the Airtable record `id` silently corrupts.
- All 5 Declined offers still show their linked Application at `Stage = Offer` instead
  of `Rejected` (5/5 — systematic, not noise). `Applications.Stage` lags
  `Offers.Status`; the Offers table is the more trustworthy source for offer outcomes,
  which is itself an input to the D3 metric definition.
- 4 interviews have `Completed On` before `Scheduled On` (temporally impossible).
- 3 offers have `Proposed Start Date` before `Offered On` (temporally impossible).
- Findings table pulled 0 records — expected, it's the write-back table and writes
  403 for us as documented.
- No dangling foreign keys anywhere (Applications→Candidates/Openings, Interviews/
  Offers→Applications, Openings→Departments all clean), no null Source/CTC/experience
  on Candidates, no CTC or negative-experience outliers, no Target-Close-before-Opened
  issues. So the corruption is narrow and specific, not pervasive — matters for how
  hard D4 should hedge.

**Funnel context (for D2 sizing, not yet a verdict)**
- 350 applications → 160 interviews → 36 offers → 26 hires.
- Interview overhead: 10 No Show + 7 Cancelled + 5 Rescheduled = 22/160 (13.8%) of
  scheduled interviews don't complete as planned — a candidate operational-efficiency
  angle independent of both VP claims.
- Job Openings: 11 Open, 8 Filled, 3 On Hold, 2 Cancelled (24 total) — haven't yet
  checked aging on the 11 Open reqs against Target Close.

## Sizing the 6 engineer-weeks (D2 candidate list)

This is the part the plan was missing: a working list of what could actually consume
the 6 weeks, each with a rough size and the evidence behind it, so the eventual "3 to
build / 3 not to build" call in D2 is a ranking of real candidates, not a first draft.
T-shirt sizing: XS ≈ 2-3 days, S ≈ 1 wk, M ≈ 1.5-2 wks, L ≈ 3-4 wks.

| # | Candidate | Size | Evidence from the data | Why it's on the list |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | Auto-sync `Applications.Stage` to `Offers.Status` (Accepted→Hired, Declined→Rejected) | S | 5/5 Declined offers still show Stage=Offer — 100% systematic, not noise | Fixes the pipeline's own bookkeeping; every other number (including the VP's own metric) is downstream of this field being trustworthy |
| B | Stale-offer expiry + recruiter nudge (flag/auto-expire Pending past a decision window) | S | 5 Pending offers aged 20–222 days; a 7-month "pending" offer is an abandoned follow-up, not a live decision | Directly targets what's inflating/obscuring the acceptance-rate number the VP wants moved — closing the loop either recovers real accepts or honestly reclassifies losses |
| C | Candidate de-dup at intake (phone+name match) | M | 6 pairs / 300 candidates (4%) are near-certain duplicates, forked across channels | Protects source attribution long-term; doesn't move either VP number directly, so it's a lower-urgency "hygiene" build unless C's true rate turns out much higher after the dedup re-check in next steps |
| D | Job-board integration as literally requested (deeper ATS/board sync) | L (unscoped — depends which boards/integration type the VP means) | Job Board is highest-volume (236 apps, 191 candidates) but lowest-converting channel (3.7% candidate→hire) — the "wide margin" claim doesn't hold, Referral ties it at the hire level | Likely the VP's literal ask but the data argues against *more volume* being the fix — candidate for "build something different" or explicit not-build, pending the Claim 1 dedup re-check |
| E | Referral program tooling (easier submission + tracking) | S–M | Referral converts 62.5% candidate→hire vs Job Board's 3.7% — the actual wide margin in this data — on only 8 candidates / 13 applications, i.e. under-invested | Best efficiency lever visible in the data; plausible "build something different" answer to the VP's Claim 1 ask instead of literal job-board integration |
| F | Interview no-show/cancellation reduction (reminders/calendar sync) | S | 22/160 scheduled interviews (13.8%) don't complete as planned | Real operational waste, independent of both VP claims — a credible 3rd item if the top ones don't fill 6 weeks |
| G | Open-requisition aging alerts | XS–S (unscoped) | Haven't pulled Target-Close aging on the 11 Open reqs yet — listed in next steps | Placeholder candidate; only keep it if the aging pull turns up something material |
| H | Offer-acceptance-rate dashboard/instrumentation (the actual D3 metric, built) | S | Today the rate only exists as an ad hoc calc off raw exports — no governed metric exists | The VP wants this number tracked and moving; it needs to exist as a real instrumented metric before anyone can "move" it |

**Preliminary read (to be revised once the next-steps checks below are done):** A + B + H
look like the non-negotiable "make the metric trustworthy" foundation (3 weeks combined)
before anything else is worth building on top of it — there's no point optimizing a number
that's currently unreliable by construction. That leaves ~3 weeks for one efficiency bet,
most likely E (referral tooling) over D (literal job-board integration), but that call
depends on the Claim 1 dedup re-check and a rough scope estimate for D — I don't have
enough to size D confidently yet, which itself may be part of the D1 verdict ("can't sign
up to a number for this until it's scoped"). C, F, G are the likely not-build/defer set,
but F could swap in for E if the referral volume turns out too small to matter even after
tooling improves it.

## Next steps before writing the deliverables

1. **Re-run Claim 1 after deduplicating the 6 candidate pairs** — does Job Board's
   26.9% / 3.7% conversion move meaningfully once duplicates collapse? Quantify the
   swing so D1's number carries an honest error bar.
2. **Decide and write the D3 metric definition** using the staleness finding: numerator
   = Accepted offers, denominator options and their edge-case handling for Pending
   offers past a decision-window threshold (propose ~30 days, need to sanity check
   against the actual Offered→Accepted/Declined turnaround time in the data first —
   haven't measured typical decision latency yet, that's a gap).
3. **Rejection-reason distribution** — pull `Applications.Rejection Reason` breakdown,
   especially for Job Board-sourced applications, to check whether high volume is
   also high-*quality* volume or whether job boards are flooding the top of funnel
   with rejects (would change the D2 recommendation on integration work).
4. **Open requisition aging** — Target Close vs today for the 11 Open reqs, by
   department/level, to see if there's a more urgent operational fire than either VP
   claim (a genuine "third finding" candidate for D1/D2).
5. **Offer Base CTC vs Job Opening Salary Band** — flag any offers outside the
   posted band; could explain some Declines and would be a concrete, cheap fix
   candidate for the "3 things to build" list.
6. **Recruiter workload** (`People.Applications as Recruiter` counts) — quick capacity
   read in case a build/no-build call should account for uneven recruiter load rather
   than pure funnel math.
7. **Quantify total record-level materiality for D4**: of 892 records pulled, how many
   are touched by at least one of the issues above (duplicates + reused IDs + stage/
   status lag + impossible dates)? Need one clean top-line "X% of records affected"
   number, not just a list of bugs.
8. **Scope candidate D (literal job-board integration) enough to size it, or say why it
   can't be sized** — the data has no signal on integration effort itself (which boards,
   what "integration" means beyond volume), so this needs to be named as a sizing gap
   in D1/D2 rather than guessed at.
9. **Re-rank the D2 candidate table above** once checks 1, 3, 4, and 8 land — the
   preliminary A+B+H foundation is fairly confident, the 4th item (E vs D vs F) is not.

## Deliverable plan (writing these after the above, per CLAUDE.md conventions)

- `docs/strategy/talentflow-q3-roadmap.md` — D1 verdicts, D2 (3 build / 3 not-build),
  D5 one-page memo. One combined doc, per the brief ("one document is fine").
- `docs/discovery/talentflow-data-quality-audit.md` — D4 in full: methodology first
  (how I went looking), then findings with materiality, then how each changes D1/D2.
- D3 (metric spec) folds into the roadmap doc as its own section, referencing the
  audit doc for the staleness evidence.
- `talentflow/findings.csv` — the required findings table (claim, metric, value,
  method, confidence) — separate file since the Findings Airtable table is read-only.
- Code/queries deliverable = existing `talentflow/*.py`, `fetch_data.sh`, this
  session's transcript. No new code needed beyond the follow-up queries above.

## Verification before finalizing numbers

- Re-run every headline number (Claim 1, Claim 2, dedup-adjusted Claim 1, staleness-
  adjusted Claim 2) one more time from raw JSON right before writing D1/D3, so the
  cited figures match what's re-runnable by the grader from the same scripts.
- Every number in the findings table gets an explicit confidence label (high/medium/
  low) tied to whether it survived a data-quality check above.

See if there's a need for some table or not. See if there's no need for any table. See if we have duplicacy of any words in the system. These can be further ideas that we can work on. Now, whatever I have said, think more along the lines in which I am trying to make you think, and then come up with the final plan before executing it. 1	# TalentFlow Q3 Roadmap — Analysis Plan
2	
3	## Context
4	
5	This is a 2-hour PM take-home: use Claude Code + the Airtable REST API to turn Acme's
6	real recruiting-ops data into a defensible Q3 roadmap. The VP of People has made two
7	claims by email (job boards drive 26.9% of hires and deserve accelerated integration
8	work; offer acceptance is ~72% and needs to move) and wants 6 engineer-weeks allocated
9	against them. Five deliverables are scored, D4 (data trust, 30 pts) weighted higher
10	than D2 (the roadmap itself, 20 pts) — the brief is explicitly rewarding skepticism
11	over a polished plan.
12	
13	All 8 tables are already pulled locally (`talentflow/data/*.json`, 892 records) and a
14	browsable version is published. This plan documents what the data deep-dive already
15	found and lays out the specific follow-up checks needed before I write the five
16	deliverables — it does not draft the deliverables themselves yet.
17	
18	## What the deep-dive already found
19	
20	**Claim 1 — "job boards bring 26.9% of hires, biggest channel by a wide margin"**
21	- The number is correct at the application level: of 26 `Hired`-stage applications,
22	  7 trace to Job Board candidates = 26.9%. But **Referral also produces exactly 7
23	  hires = 26.9%** — they're tied, not "a wide margin." Job Board only leads on raw
24	  volume (236 of 350 applications; 191 of 300 candidates).
25	- Candidate→hire conversion tells the opposite story: Job Board converts 7/191 = 3.7%.
26	  Referral converts 5/8 = 62.5% (candidate-level; some candidates have 2 applications,
27	  which is why app-level and candidate-level hire counts differ slightly — 26 vs 24).
28	  Agency 11.4%, Career Site 16.1%, LinkedIn 9.7%, Campus 0/4.
29	- Reading: job boards win on volume, not efficiency. "Bring forward the integration"
30	  is arguable but the VP's own framing ("wide margin") doesn't survive contact with
31	  the data — this needs to be said plainly in D1.
32	
33	**Claim 2 — "offer acceptance rate is ~72%"**
34	- 36 offers total: 26 Accepted, 5 Declined, 5 Pending. 26/36 = 72.2% — matches the VP
35	  exactly, but only if Pending offers are counted as failures in the denominator.
36	- Exclude Pending (treat as still-undecided): 26/31 = 83.9%. An 11.7-point swing on
37	  one definitional choice — this is the crux of D3.
38	- The 5 "Pending" offers are 20 to **222 days old** (as of the latest data ~2026-08-27).
39	  A 7-month-old "pending" offer is not a live decision in progress, it's abandoned and
40	  never closed out. Treating it as genuinely pending (and excluding it) inflates the
41	  acceptance rate; treating it as a failure (72.2%) is closer to true but conflates
42	  "candidate said no" with "nobody ever closed the loop." Neither raw number is fully
43	  trustworthy without a staleness rule — this is what D3 needs to fix.
44	
45	**Data-quality issues found so far (candidates for D4, with materiality)**
46	- 6 pairs of candidate records (12 of 300 = 4%) share identical phone + full name but
47	  different email and Candidate ID — near-certain duplicate people, likely re-applying
48	  under a different email. This directly risks inflating Job Board's application/
49	  candidate counts and understating true per-channel conversion (need to re-run Claim 1
50	  after collapsing these).
51	- 4 Application IDs (APP-00001, 00005, 00007, 00010) are each reused across two
52	  completely different application records (different candidates, openings, stages).
53	  `Application ID` is not a safe join key — anything downstream that joins on it
54	  instead of the Airtable record `id` silently corrupts.
55	- All 5 Declined offers still show their linked Application at `Stage = Offer` instead
56	  of `Rejected` (5/5 — systematic, not noise). `Applications.Stage` lags
57	  `Offers.Status`; the Offers table is the more trustworthy source for offer outcomes,
58	  which is itself an input to the D3 metric definition.
59	- 4 interviews have `Completed On` before `Scheduled On` (temporally impossible).
60	- 3 offers have `Proposed Start Date` before `Offered On` (temporally impossible).
61	- Findings table pulled 0 records — expected, it's the write-back table and writes
62	  403 for us as documented.
63	- No dangling foreign keys anywhere (Applications→Candidates/Openings, Interviews/
64	  Offers→Applications, Openings→Departments all clean), no null Source/CTC/experience
65	  on Candidates, no CTC or negative-experience outliers, no Target-Close-before-Opened
66	  issues. So the corruption is narrow and specific, not pervasive — matters for how
67	  hard D4 should hedge.
68	
69	**Funnel context (for D2 sizing, not yet a verdict)**
70	- 350 applications → 160 interviews → 36 offers → 26 hires.
71	- Interview overhead: 10 No Show + 7 Cancelled + 5 Rescheduled = 22/160 (13.8%) of
72	  scheduled interviews don't complete as planned — a candidate operational-efficiency
73	  angle independent of both VP claims.
74	- Job Openings: 11 Open, 8 Filled, 3 On Hold, 2 Cancelled (24 total) — haven't yet
75	  checked aging on the 11 Open reqs against Target Close.
76	
77	## Sizing the 6 engineer-weeks (D2 candidate list)
78	
79	This is the part the plan was missing: a working list of what could actually consume
80	the 6 weeks, each with a rough size and the evidence behind it, so the eventual "3 to
81	build / 3 not to build" call in D2 is a ranking of real candidates, not a first draft.
82	T-shirt sizing: XS ≈ 2-3 days, S ≈ 1 wk, M ≈ 1.5-2 wks, L ≈ 3-4 wks.
83	
84	| # | Candidate | Size | Evidence from the data | Why it's on the list |
85	|---|---|---|---|---|
86	| A | Auto-sync `Applications.Stage` to `Offers.Status` (Accepted→Hired, Declined→Rejected) | S | 5/5 Declined offers still show Stage=Offer — 100% systematic, not noise | Fixes the pipeline's own bookkeeping; every other number (including the VP's own metric) is downstream of this field being trustworthy |
87	| B | Stale-offer expiry + recruiter nudge (flag/auto-expire Pending past a decision window) | S | 5 Pending offers aged 20–222 days; a 7-month "pending" offer is an abandoned follow-up, not a live decision | Directly targets what's inflating/obscuring the acceptance-rate number the VP wants moved — closing the loop either recovers real accepts or honestly reclassifies losses |
88	| C | Candidate de-dup at intake (phone+name match) | M | 6 pairs / 300 candidates (4%) are near-certain duplicates, forked across channels | Protects source attribution long-term; doesn't move either VP number directly, so it's a lower-urgency "hygiene" build unless C's true rate turns out much higher after the dedup re-check in next steps |
89	| D | Job-board integration as literally requested (deeper ATS/board sync) | L (unscoped — depends which boards/integration type the VP means) | Job Board is highest-volume (236 apps, 191 candidates) but lowest-converting channel (3.7% candidate→hire) — the "wide margin" claim doesn't hold, Referral ties it at the hire level | Likely the VP's literal ask but the data argues against *more volume* being the fix — candidate for "build something different" or explicit not-build, pending the Claim 1 dedup re-check |
90	| E | Referral program tooling (easier submission + tracking) | S–M | Referral converts 62.5% candidate→hire vs Job Board's 3.7% — the actual wide margin in this data — on only 8 candidates / 13 applications, i.e. under-invested | Best efficiency lever visible in the data; plausible "build something different" answer to the VP's Claim 1 ask instead of literal job-board integration |
91	| F | Interview no-show/cancellation reduction (reminders/calendar sync) | S | 22/160 scheduled interviews (13.8%) don't complete as planned | Real operational waste, independent of both VP claims — a credible 3rd item if the top ones don't fill 6 weeks |
92	| G | Open-requisition aging alerts | XS–S (unscoped) | Haven't pulled Target-Close aging on the 11 Open reqs yet — listed in next steps | Placeholder candidate; only keep it if the aging pull turns up something material |
93	| H | Offer-acceptance-rate dashboard/instrumentation (the actual D3 metric, built) | S | Today the rate only exists as an ad hoc calc off raw exports — no governed metric exists | The VP wants this number tracked and moving; it needs to exist as a real instrumented metric before anyone can "move" it |
94	
95	**Preliminary read (to be revised once the next-steps checks below are done):** A + B + H
96	look like the non-negotiable "make the metric trustworthy" foundation (3 weeks combined)
97	before anything else is worth building on top of it — there's no point optimizing a number
98	that's currently unreliable by construction. That leaves ~3 weeks for one efficiency bet,
99	most likely E (referral tooling) over D (literal job-board integration), but that call
100	depends on the Claim 1 dedup re-check and a rough scope estimate for D — I don't have
101	enough to size D confidently yet, which itself may be part of the D1 verdict ("can't sign
102	up to a number for this until it's scoped"). C, F, G are the likely not-build/defer set,
103	but F could swap in for E if the referral volume turns out too small to matter even after
104	tooling improves it.
105	
106	## Next steps before writing the deliverables
107	
108	1. **Re-run Claim 1 after deduplicating the 6 candidate pairs** — does Job Board's
109	   26.9% / 3.7% conversion move meaningfully once duplicates collapse? Quantify the
110	   swing so D1's number carries an honest error bar.
111	2. **Decide and write the D3 metric definition** using the staleness finding: numerator
112	   = Accepted offers, denominator options and their edge-case handling for Pending
113	   offers past a decision-window threshold (propose ~30 days, need to sanity check
114	   against the actual Offered→Accepted/Declined turnaround time in the data first —
115	   haven't measured typical decision latency yet, that's a gap).
116	3. **Rejection-reason distribution** — pull `Applications.Rejection Reason` breakdown,
117	   especially for Job Board-sourced applications, to check whether high volume is
118	   also high-*quality* volume or whether job boards are flooding the top of funnel
119	   with rejects (would change the D2 recommendation on integration work).
120	4. **Open requisition aging** — Target Close vs today for the 11 Open reqs, by
121	   department/level, to see if there's a more urgent operational fire than either VP
122	   claim (a genuine "third finding" candidate for D1/D2).
123	5. **Offer Base CTC vs Job Opening Salary Band** — flag any offers outside the
124	   posted band; could explain some Declines and would be a concrete, cheap fix
125	   candidate for the "3 things to build" list.
126	6. **Recruiter workload** (`People.Applications as Recruiter` counts) — quick capacity
127	   read in case a build/no-build call should account for uneven recruiter load rather
128	   than pure funnel math.
129	7. **Quantify total record-level materiality for D4**: of 892 records pulled, how many
130	   are touched by at least one of the issues above (duplicates + reused IDs + stage/
131	   status lag + impossible dates)? Need one clean top-line "X% of records affected"
132	   number, not just a list of bugs.
133	8. **Scope candidate D (literal job-board integration) enough to size it, or say why it
134	   can't be sized** — the data has no signal on integration effort itself (which boards,
135	   what "integration" means beyond volume), so this needs to be named as a sizing gap
136	   in D1/D2 rather than guessed at.
137	9. **Re-rank the D2 candidate table above** once checks 1, 3, 4, and 8 land — the
138	   preliminary A+B+H foundation is fairly confident, the 4th item (E vs D vs F) is not.
139	
140	## Deliverable plan (writing these after the above, per CLAUDE.md conventions)
141	
142	- `docs/strategy/talentflow-q3-roadmap.md` — D1 verdicts, D2 (3 build / 3 not-build),
143	  D5 one-page memo. One combined doc, per the brief ("one document is fine").

# TalentFlow Q3 Roadmap — Analysis Plan

## Context

This is a 2-hour PM take-home: use Claude Code + the Airtable REST API to turn Acme's
real recruiting-ops data into a defensible Q3 roadmap. The VP of People has made two
claims by email (job boards drive 26.9% of hires and deserve accelerated integration
work; offer acceptance is ~72% and needs to move) and wants 6 engineer-weeks allocated
against them. Five deliverables are scored, D4 (data trust, 30 pts) weighted higher
than D2 (the roadmap itself, 20 pts) — the brief is explicitly rewarding skepticism
over a polished plan.

All 8 tables are already pulled locally (`talentflow/data/*.json`, 892 records) and a
browsable version is published. This plan documents what the data deep-dive already
found and lays out the specific follow-up checks needed before I write the five
deliverables — it does not draft the deliverables themselves yet.

## What the deep-dive already found

**Claim 1 — "job boards bring 26.9% of hires, biggest channel by a wide margin"**
- The number is correct at the application level: of 26 `Hired`-stage applications,
  7 trace to Job Board candidates = 26.9%. But **Referral also produces exactly 7
  hires = 26.9%** — they're tied, not "a wide margin." Job Board only leads on raw
  volume (236 of 350 applications; 191 of 300 candidates).
- Candidate→hire conversion tells the opposite story: Job Board converts 7/191 = 3.7%.
  Referral converts 5/8 = 62.5% (candidate-level; some candidates have 2 applications,
  which is why app-level and candidate-level hire counts differ slightly — 26 vs 24).
  Agency 11.4%, Career Site 16.1%, LinkedIn 9.7%, Campus 0/4.
- Reading: job boards win on volume, not efficiency. "Bring forward the integration"
  is arguable but the VP's own framing ("wide margin") doesn't survive contact with
  the data — this needs to be said plainly in D1.

**Claim 2 — "offer acceptance rate is ~72%"**
- 36 offers total: 26 Accepted, 5 Declined, 5 Pending. 26/36 = 72.2% — matches the VP
  exactly, but only if Pending offers are counted as failures in the denominator.
- Exclude Pending (treat as still-undecided): 26/31 = 83.9%. An 11.7-point swing on
  one definitional choice — this is the crux of D3.
- The 5 "Pending" offers are 20 to **222 days old** (as of the latest data ~2026-08-27).
  A 7-month-old "pending" offer is not a live decision in progress, it's abandoned and
  never closed out. Treating it as genuinely pending (and excluding it) inflates the
  acceptance rate; treating it as a failure (72.2%) is closer to true but conflates
  "candidate said no" with "nobody ever closed the loop." Neither raw number is fully
  trustworthy without a staleness rule — this is what D3 needs to fix.

**Data-quality issues found so far (candidates for D4, with materiality)**
- 6 pairs of candidate records (12 of 300 = 4%) share identical phone + full name but
  different email and Candidate ID — near-certain duplicate people, likely re-applying
  under a different email. This directly risks inflating Job Board's application/
  candidate counts and understating true per-channel conversion (need to re-run Claim 1
  after collapsing these).
- 4 Application IDs (APP-00001, 00005, 00007, 00010) are each reused across two
  completely different application records (different candidates, openings, stages).
  `Application ID` is not a safe join key — anything downstream that joins on it
  instead of the Airtable record `id` silently corrupts.
- All 5 Declined offers still show their linked Application at `Stage = Offer` instead
  of `Rejected` (5/5 — systematic, not noise). `Applications.Stage` lags
  `Offers.Status`; the Offers table is the more trustworthy source for offer outcomes,
  which is itself an input to the D3 metric definition.
- 4 interviews have `Completed On` before `Scheduled On` (temporally impossible).
- 3 offers have `Proposed Start Date` before `Offered On` (temporally impossible).
- Findings table pulled 0 records — expected, it's the write-back table and writes
  403 for us as documented.
- No dangling foreign keys anywhere (Applications→Candidates/Openings, Interviews/
  Offers→Applications, Openings→Departments all clean), no null Source/CTC/experience
  on Candidates, no CTC or negative-experience outliers, no Target-Close-before-Opened
  issues. So the corruption is narrow and specific, not pervasive — matters for how
  hard D4 should hedge.

**Funnel context (for D2 sizing, not yet a verdict)**
- 350 applications → 160 interviews → 36 offers → 26 hires.
- Interview overhead: 10 No Show + 7 Cancelled + 5 Rescheduled = 22/160 (13.8%) of
  scheduled interviews don't complete as planned — a candidate operational-efficiency
  angle independent of both VP claims.
- Job Openings: 11 Open, 8 Filled, 3 On Hold, 2 Cancelled (24 total) — haven't yet
  checked aging on the 11 Open reqs against Target Close.

## Sizing the 6 engineer-weeks (D2 candidate list)

This is the part the plan was missing: a working list of what could actually consume
the 6 weeks, each with a rough size and the evidence behind it, so the eventual "3 to
build / 3 not to build" call in D2 is a ranking of real candidates, not a first draft.
T-shirt sizing: XS ≈ 2-3 days, S ≈ 1 wk, M ≈ 1.5-2 wks, L ≈ 3-4 wks.

| # | Candidate | Size | Evidence from the data | Why it's on the list |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | Auto-sync `Applications.Stage` to `Offers.Status` (Accepted→Hired, Declined→Rejected) | S | 5/5 Declined offers still show Stage=Offer — 100% systematic, not noise | Fixes the pipeline's own bookkeeping; every other number (including the VP's own metric) is downstream of this field being trustworthy |
| B | Stale-offer expiry + recruiter nudge (flag/auto-expire Pending past a decision window) | S | 5 Pending offers aged 20–222 days; a 7-month "pending" offer is an abandoned follow-up, not a live decision | Directly targets what's inflating/obscuring the acceptance-rate number the VP wants moved — closing the loop either recovers real accepts or honestly reclassifies losses |
| C | Candidate de-dup at intake (phone+name match) | M | 6 pairs / 300 candidates (4%) are near-certain duplicates, forked across channels | Protects source attribution long-term; doesn't move either VP number directly, so it's a lower-urgency "hygiene" build unless C's true rate turns out much higher after the dedup re-check in next steps |
| D | Job-board integration as literally requested (deeper ATS/board sync) | L (unscoped — depends which boards/integration type the VP means) | Job Board is highest-volume (236 apps, 191 candidates) but lowest-converting channel (3.7% candidate→hire) — the "wide margin" claim doesn't hold, Referral ties it at the hire level | Likely the VP's literal ask but the data argues against *more volume* being the fix — candidate for "build something different" or explicit not-build, pending the Claim 1 dedup re-check |
| E | Referral program tooling (easier submission + tracking) | S–M | Referral converts 62.5% candidate→hire vs Job Board's 3.7% — the actual wide margin in this data — on only 8 candidates / 13 applications, i.e. under-invested | Best efficiency lever visible in the data; plausible "build something different" answer to the VP's Claim 1 ask instead of literal job-board integration |
| F | Interview no-show/cancellation reduction (reminders/calendar sync) | S | 22/160 scheduled interviews (13.8%) don't complete as planned | Real operational waste, independent of both VP claims — a credible 3rd item if the top ones don't fill 6 weeks |
| G | Open-requisition aging alerts | XS–S (unscoped) | Haven't pulled Target-Close aging on the 11 Open reqs yet — listed in next steps | Placeholder candidate; only keep it if the aging pull turns up something material |
| H | Offer-acceptance-rate dashboard/instrumentation (the actual D3 metric, built) | S | Today the rate only exists as an ad hoc calc off raw exports — no governed metric exists | The VP wants this number tracked and moving; it needs to exist as a real instrumented metric before anyone can "move" it |

**Preliminary read (to be revised once the next-steps checks below are done):** A + B + H
look like the non-negotiable "make the metric trustworthy" foundation (3 weeks combined)
before anything else is worth building on top of it — there's no point optimizing a number
that's currently unreliable by construction. That leaves ~3 weeks for one efficiency bet,
most likely E (referral tooling) over D (literal job-board integration), but that call
depends on the Claim 1 dedup re-check and a rough scope estimate for D — I don't have
enough to size D confidently yet, which itself may be part of the D1 verdict ("can't sign
up to a number for this until it's scoped"). C, F, G are the likely not-build/defer set,
but F could swap in for E if the referral volume turns out too small to matter even after
tooling improves it.

## Next steps before writing the deliverables

1. **Re-run Claim 1 after deduplicating the 6 candidate pairs** — does Job Board's
   26.9% / 3.7% conversion move meaningfully once duplicates collapse? Quantify the
   swing so D1's number carries an honest error bar.
2. **Decide and write the D3 metric definition** using the staleness finding: numerator
   = Accepted offers, denominator options and their edge-case handling for Pending
   offers past a decision-window threshold (propose ~30 days, need to sanity check
   against the actual Offered→Accepted/Declined turnaround time in the data first —
   haven't measured typical decision latency yet, that's a gap).
3. **Rejection-reason distribution** — pull `Applications.Rejection Reason` breakdown,
   especially for Job Board-sourced applications, to check whether high volume is
   also high-*quality* volume or whether job boards are flooding the top of funnel
   with rejects (would change the D2 recommendation on integration work).
4. **Open requisition aging** — Target Close vs today for the 11 Open reqs, by
   department/level, to see if there's a more urgent operational fire than either VP
   claim (a genuine "third finding" candidate for D1/D2).
5. **Offer Base CTC vs Job Opening Salary Band** — flag any offers outside the
   posted band; could explain some Declines and would be a concrete, cheap fix
   candidate for the "3 things to build" list.
6. **Recruiter workload** (`People.Applications as Recruiter` counts) — quick capacity
   read in case a build/no-build call should account for uneven recruiter load rather
   than pure funnel math.
7. **Quantify total record-level materiality for D4**: of 892 records pulled, how many
   are touched by at least one of the issues above (duplicates + reused IDs + stage/
   status lag + impossible dates)? Need one clean top-line "X% of records affected"
   number, not just a list of bugs.
8. **Scope candidate D (literal job-board integration) enough to size it, or say why it
   can't be sized** — the data has no signal on integration effort itself (which boards,
   what "integration" means beyond volume), so this needs to be named as a sizing gap
   in D1/D2 rather than guessed at.
9. **Re-rank the D2 candidate table above** once checks 1, 3, 4, and 8 land — the
   preliminary A+B+H foundation is fairly confident, the 4th item (E vs D vs F) is not.

## Deliverable plan (writing these after the above, per CLAUDE.md conventions)

- `docs/strategy/talentflow-q3-roadmap.md` — D1 verdicts, D2 (3 build / 3 not-build),
  D5 one-page memo. One combined doc, per the brief ("one document is fine").
- `docs/discovery/talentflow-data-quality-audit.md` — D4 in full: methodology first
  (how I went looking), then findings with materiality, then how each changes D1/D2.
- D3 (metric spec) folds into the roadmap doc as its own section, referencing the
  audit doc for the staleness evidence.
- `talentflow/findings.csv` — the required findings table (claim, metric, value,
  method, confidence) — separate file since the Findings Airtable table is read-only.
- Code/queries deliverable = existing `talentflow/*.py`, `fetch_data.sh`, this
  session's transcript. No new code needed beyond the follow-up queries above.

## Verification before finalizing numbers

- Re-run every headline number (Claim 1, Claim 2, dedup-adjusted Claim 1, staleness-
  adjusted Claim 2) one more time from raw JSON right before writing D1/D3, so the
  cited figures match what's re-runnable by the grader from the same scripts.
- Every number in the findings table gets an explicit confidence label (high/medium/
  low) tied to whether it survived a data-quality check above.

## Table interconnection audit — current state vs recommended state

You asked specifically about the Interviews→Interviewer / Applications link and whether
pointers between tables are actually synchronized. I checked this exhaustively (every
record, not a sample) rather than assuming. Two different things came back, and they
point in opposite directions:

**Current state, verified against all records: the links themselves are 100% intact.**
I checked every forward/reverse link pair Airtable exposes — Interviews.Interviewer ↔
People.Interviews, Interviews.Application ↔ Applications.Interviews, Applications.Recruiter
↔ People["Applications as Recruiter"], Applications.Candidate ↔ Candidates.Applications,
Applications.Opening ↔ JobOpenings.Applications, Offers.Application ↔ Applications.Offers,
JobOpenings.Department ↔ Departments["Job Openings"], People.Department ↔ Departments.People,
JobOpenings.Recruiter ↔ People["Reqs as Recruiter"], JobOpenings.HiringManager ↔
People["Reqs as Hiring Manager"] — **0 mismatches across all of them.** So if you searched
an Interview ID inside Applications.Interviews and it wasn't there, that's not what's
happening — the record-ID pointers are clean. Airtable maintains these automatically and
the data respects it everywhere.

**What's actually wrong — and it's a bigger finding than a broken pointer — is that the
*people assigned* to a given piece of work don't line up with each other's department at
all, system-wide, not just for interviewers:**

| Relationship checked | Same department | Different department | Mismatch rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interview's Interviewer vs the Opening being interviewed for | 22 | 138 | **86%** |
| Application's Recruiter vs the Opening's department | 80 | 270 | **77%** |
| Job Opening's Hiring Manager vs the Opening's own department | 3 | 21 | **87%** |
| Application's Recruiter vs that application's Interviewer (same app) | 0 same person, ever | 160 / 160 | **100%** — recruiter and interviewer are never the same person on any of the 160 interviews |

This is why you noticed it on Interviewer specifically — it's the most visible instance of
a pattern that runs through Recruiter and Hiring Manager assignment too. I also checked
whether this is just because there aren't enough people to go around: there are only 6
Interviewers / 4 Recruiters / 4 Hiring Managers for 8 departments, so *some* cross-department
assignment is structurally forced — but even departments that have their own dedicated
interviewer still get cross-department assignments most of the time, so scarcity doesn't
explain an 86% mismatch rate. Every person's Role field is also perfectly single-purpose
(a Recruiter never interviews, an Interviewer never recruits, 0 exceptions) — that plus the
random-looking department assignment reads like a data-generation artifact (roles and
department links were sampled independently of each other) rather than an organic
org chart. I'm flagging this as a trust caveat, not asserting certainty either way.

**Recommended state:** before any interviewer-, recruiter-, or hiring-manager-level cut is
used to justify a decision, this needs to be named explicitly: either (a) this is how Acme
actually staffs hiring — a floating interviewer/recruiter pool, not department-dedicated,
which is a legitimate model and just needs to be understood before drawing conclusions from
department-level people-cuts, or (b) it's a seeding/sync artifact in this specific export and
person-level cuts should be treated as low-confidence until confirmed with Acme. I can't tell
which from the data alone — this goes in D4 as an open question, not a resolved bug, and it
gates how much weight cross-cuts #14–16 below (interviewer calibration, cross-dept quality
impact) should carry.

**One more synchronization pattern worth surfacing while on this topic:** `Applications.Status`
is not simply derived from `Stage` — for the 10 applications sitting at `Stage = Offer`,
`Status` splits cleanly into 5×(Active, linked Offer=Pending) and 5×(Closed, linked
Offer=Declined) — Status tracks the *Offer* record's resolution faithfully even when Stage
itself fails to advance to Rejected. So `Status` is actually the more reliable "is this
decided" signal; `Stage`'s specific bucket (Hired vs Rejected) is what lags. That refines the
earlier D3-relevant finding: don't discard Stage/Status as broken, use Status for "is this
closed" and Offers.Status as ground truth for "closed how."

## Multi-table cross-cut plan — going past the two claims

Point taken that the current 6-week candidate list (A–H above) is a set of one-week fixes,
not big thinking. The two VP claims only required 2-3 tables joined one way. Getting to
sharper, more ambitious project ideas means actually multiplying the tables against each
other the way you described — funnel × department × source × level × time × people — before
guessing what to build. Below is the plan for that, not the execution.

**Step 0 — lock the identity/key model first, before any cross-cut, so nothing downstream
inherits an error:**
- Canonical join key everywhere is the Airtable record `id`, never a business string ID —
  already proven necessary (4 `Application ID` values are each reused by two unrelated
  records; joining on the string ID silently merges the wrong rows).
- Canonical **person** identity for Candidates is not yet decided. 6 of 300 candidate
  records (4%) are near-certain duplicates of the same physical person (identical phone +
  name, different email/record). Before any candidate-level (not application-level) funnel
  or source cut runs, I need to pick a merge rule (phone-normalized match, tie-broken by
  name) and produce both a raw view and a canonical-person view, so every cross-cut below
  can report "as recorded" and "as-deduped" side by side rather than silently picking one.
- People (14 rows) needs no dedup — checked, clean, one row per person, roles mutually
  exclusive.
- Schema redundancy check, so I don't build 20 tables on top of columns that are secretly
  the same thing: `Status` fields exist in three unrelated tables (Applications: Active/
  Closed; Job Openings: Open/Filled/On Hold/Cancelled; Offers: Pending/Accepted/Declined) —
  same column name, three different enumerations, not mergeable, just needs table-qualified
  naming so a cross-cut never accidentally groups by the wrong "Status." `Outcome` vs
  `Recommendation` on Interviews are genuinely different axes (process vs verdict) — keep
  both. No column found so far is pure duplication of another; will re-check once the
  Rejection Reason distribution (next steps #3) is in.

**Step 1 — the cross-cut catalog.** Each row is one self-contained, deterministic
computation (funnel counts + % drop + median days between stages, where time applies).
Grouped by what they're meant to surface:

*Funnel × dimension × time*
1. Department × Stage funnel (counts, % drop per stage, median days-in-stage)
2. Source × Stage funnel + time-to-each-stage
3. Department × Source interaction (does a given source convert differently by department?)
4. Level (Junior/Mid/Senior, from Job Openings.Level) × Stage funnel
5. Employment Type (Full-time/Part-time/Contract) × Stage funnel
6. Candidate City × Stage funnel (geographic conversion / relocation friction)
7. Recruiter × Stage funnel + workload-adjusted time-in-stage
8. Interview Round × Outcome × Recommendation (where in the interview loop do people
   actually get filtered)

*Candidate segment × offer outcome*
9. Notice Period bucket (0–15/16–30/31–60/61–90/90+ days) × Level × Offer-Accept rate
10. Expected-vs-Current CTC gap bucket (the raise % a candidate is asking for) × Accept rate
11. Offer Base CTC vs that Opening's Salary Band position (below/within/above band) × Accept rate
12. Years-experience bucket × Level applied-for (are we mis-leveling candidates relative to
    their experience, and does that predict rejection or decline?)
13. Candidate City × Offer-Accept rate

*Interviewer/quality lens (read together with the department-affinity caveat above)*
14. Interviewer × avg Score × Recommendation mix × actual downstream Outcome (a calibration
    check: does this interviewer's "Hire" call actually predict getting hired, or is one
    person systematically harsher/more lenient than the rest of the panel?)
15. Round × avg Score trend (do scores genuinely climb Screen→Technical→Bar Raiser, or is
    an early round just noise that gets overridden later?)
16. Same-department vs cross-department interview assignment × avg Score / Outcome — does
    the affinity break found above actually correlate with worse or more volatile outcomes,
    or does it wash out?

*Operational timing*
17. Time-in-stage waterfall (Applied→Screened→Interview→Offer→Closed), department-level
    medians *and* the outlier tail — find the real bottleneck instead of assuming one
18. Requisition aging: Opened On → Target Close → actual Filled date, by department/level
19. Interview scheduling lead time (Applied On → First Interview On) and offer lead time
    (Final Interview On → Offered On), by department/source
20. Monthly/quarterly trend of applications, hires, and acceptance rate — is either VP claim
    a persistent pattern or one noisy quarter?

*Referral network*
21. `Referred By` chains — who refers, how many of their referrals convert, is there a
    concentrated set of "super-referrers" worth building a program around (feeds directly
    into candidate E from the current list, with actual evidence behind the sizing)
22. Rejection Reason × Source × Department (does Job Board's volume convert to real
    pipeline or mostly to one dominant rejection reason — directly informs the D pick)

**Step 2 — challenger pass on every cut, not just a spot-check on the two VP numbers.**
For each of the ~20 results above:
- Recompute the headline number a second, differently-coded way (e.g. pandas groupby vs a
  manual dict aggregation) — must match exactly before it's accepted.
- Re-run it once on the raw candidate identities and once on the deduped/canonical view from
  Step 0, and report the delta — if a conclusion flips between the two, that conclusion is
  not usable as-is and gets flagged, not quietly resolved in whichever direction is more
  convenient.
- Any cell with n < 10 gets marked low-confidence — with 300 candidates / 36 offers / 160
  interviews, several of the 3-way cuts above (e.g. Level × Notice-Period-bucket × Accept)
  will have thin cells; the catalog is honest that some of these will come back "not enough
  data to say," which is itself a usable answer.
- One adversarial sentence per surviving finding: "this could be wrong because ___" —
  before it goes in front of anyone.

**Step 3 — how I'd actually build this (once you approve), addressing the orchestration
ask directly:** the arithmetic has to be plain, deterministic Python reading the local
JSON/CSV — no step where a model is asked to eyeball numbers and report them, that's exactly
the hallucination risk a challenger pass exists to catch. Where parallelism helps is in
*producing* the ~20 scripts quickly: I'd fan out via the Agent tool, one agent per cross-cut
spec above, each agent writes one small, single-purpose Python script under
`talentflow/analysis/`, runs it against the local data, and returns the resulting table plus
a 2-3 sentence finding — never a number typed from memory. A second pass (challenger, per
Step 2) independently re-derives each headline number before it's accepted into the
synthesis. Outputs: one CSV per cross-cut under `talentflow/analysis/`, plus a single
lightweight HTML summary (top-line findings first, then per-cut drill-down tables) in the
same style as the data browser already published — this one built for analysis, not raw
record browsing.

**Step 4 — only after Steps 1-3 land, revisit the 6-engineer-week list.** The current
A–H candidates are individually real but uniformly small (single-recruiter-week scale). Once
the department/source/level/time cross-cuts are in, I expect sharper and larger candidates
to surface — e.g. if #17 finds one specific stage is the true department-level bottleneck
(not assumed), the fix is a targeted process/tooling change sized to that evidence, not a
generic "add reminders" item; if #14/#16 show real interviewer-calibration problems, a
scoring/calibration system is a legitimately bigger (2-3 week) build than anything on the
current list. I'm not pre-committing to specific new candidates here — that's what Steps 1-3
are for — but the list you saw is a floor, not the ceiling, and I expect it to change.

import json, math
from collections import Counter
from datetime import date

def wilson_ci(x, n, z=1.96):
    if n == 0: return (None, None)
    phat = x/n
    denom = 1 + z**2/n
    center = (phat + z**2/(2*n)) / denom
    halfwidth = z*math.sqrt(phat*(1-phat)/n + z**2/(4*n**2)) / denom
    return (round((center-halfwidth)*100,1), round((center+halfwidth)*100,1))

print("=== Wilson 95% CI: offer acceptance rate under both definitions ===")

## Correctness re-check — running this as a proficient analyst would, not a spreadsheet pass

You were right to push back. I went back through the headline numbers the way a rigorous
analyst actually should, before touching the bigger cross-cut catalog — and it changed two
of them. Recording what changed and why, plus the standing checks this means every cut
below has to pass, not just the two VP claims.

**1. The referral-vs-job-board finding was contaminated by the duplicate-candidate issue —
not just adjacent to it.** Of the 6 duplicate-phone candidate pairs, 2 span Job Board and
Referral for the *same physical person* — and in both cases, that person's Job Board
application was rejected and their Referral application was the one that got hired (Varun
Sharma: Job Board rejected 2025-04-08, Referral hired 2026-06-07; Aarav Menon: Referral
hired 2026-04-14, Job Board rejected 2026-05-30, opposite order). That means 2 of the 5
candidate-level Referral hires (40% of them) are people who also have a Job Board record —
the "referral converts 8x better" finding was standing partly on identity confusion, not
just noise. I re-ran it with the duplicates merged (first-touch attribution — the source of
whichever record was created earliest for that person):

| View | Job Board share of hires | Job Board candidate-conversion | Referral share of hires | Referral candidate-conversion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Raw (as recorded, hired-touch) | 26.9% (tied w/ Referral) | 3.7% | 26.9% (tied w/ Job Board) | 62.5% |
| Deduped, first-touch attribution | **33.3%** (clear largest) | 4.3% | 16.7% | 57.1% |

Attribution methodology (first-touch vs "credit whichever record actually converted") is a
real, named choice here, not a bug to resolve — first-touch is the standard marketing-
attribution convention and I'd default to it, but it needs to be stated as an assumption in
D1, not hidden. **What holds up under both views: Job Board is the volume leader and converts
far worse per-candidate than Referral, in both raw and deduped numbers.** What does *not*
hold up: the specific claim that the two channels are tied at 26.9% of hires — that tie was
an artifact of counting the same person under two source labels; deduped, Job Board is
unambiguously ahead on hire share. This changes the D1 verdict language: it's not "the VP's
'wide margin' claim is false," it's "the VP's *volume* framing is directionally fine, the
*efficiency* framing is the real story, and the exact 26.9% figure isn't robust to how you
resolve 12 duplicate records."

**2. Both headline rates are noisier than their point estimates suggest — checked with
Wilson confidence intervals, not just the raw percentage:**

| Number | Point estimate | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| Offer acceptance, Pending=fail | 72.2% (26/36) | **[56.0%, 84.2%]** |
| Offer acceptance, Pending excluded | 83.9% (26/31) | **[67.4%, 92.9%]** |
| Job Board candidate-conversion | 3.7% (7/191) | [1.8%, 7.4%] |
| Referral candidate-conversion (raw) | 62.5% (5/8) | **[30.6%, 86.3%]** |

The two offer-acceptance CIs **overlap** (56-84% vs 67-93%, overlapping 67-84%) — at n=36
offers, the "12-point swing from one definitional choice" I flagged earlier is not
statistically distinguishable from sampling noise. That doesn't make the definitional
question unimportant (D3 still needs one canonical rule), but it means neither 72.2% nor
83.9% should be presented to the VP as a precise numeryou'd bet the plan on — this is the
single most important thing to say about Claim 2, and it belongs in D3's "what the
dashboard shows when the answer is ambiguous" requirement directly: **show the rate with its
n and interval, never a bare percentage, given how few offers there are.**
Referral's conversion-rate CI is enormous ([30.6%, 86.3%]) because n=8 — Job Board being much
worse is solid (the CIs don't come close to overlapping), but the *exact size* of Referral's
advantage is not something 8 data points can tell you. Directionally real, precisely
unknowable — say both parts.

**3. Department-level funnels will be underpowered at full stage granularity.** Applications
per department range from 23 (Finance) to 69 (Sales) across 7 Stage values — that's 3 to 10
per stage per department on average, most cells in single digits before any second dimension
(source, level) is added. Any department × stage cross-cut needs to collapse to 3-4 coarse
buckets (e.g. Active-early / Active-late / Hired / Rejected+Withdrawn) rather than the full
7-value Stage field, or it will report noise as pattern. This changes how cross-cuts #1, #3,
#4, #7 in the catalog below need to be built, not whether to build them.

**4. Right-censoring: 105 of 350 applications (30%) are still open (`Status = Active`), and
they're heavily concentrated in the most recent months** — 23 opened in June 2026 alone, 13
in July, 9 in August, vs. single digits per month before 2026-04. Any month-over-month trend
in hire rate or acceptance rate will look mechanically worse for recent months purely because
those cohorts haven't finished flowing through the pipeline yet, not because anything
actually got worse. This directly matters for cross-cut #20 (monthly trend) and for reading
the VP's own "the board is asking about it, it needs moving" framing — if the VP is looking
at a recent-quarter snapshot, part of what they're seeing may be pipeline lag, not a real
decline. The fix: exclude the most recent 2-3 months from any trend claim (cohorts need time
to mature/resolve), or use time-to-event framing instead of a point-in-time rate. This needs
to be checked *before* claiming the rate has moved at all — which is possible the VP hasn't
done either.

**Standing rules this sets for every cross-cut in the catalog below** (not just the two VP
claims): (a) report every rate with its n and a Wilson CI, never a bare percentage; (b) check
expected cell size before running any 2+ dimension cut, and collapse categories rather than
report single-digit cells as if they were signal; (c) test source/channel-based findings
against both raw and duplicate-resolved candidate identity, the way Claim 1 just was; (d)
exclude or clearly flag any time-based cut's most recent 2-3 months for right-censoring.

content.text:
I re-ran the analysis with the rigor you were pushing for, and it actually changed two headline conclusions — worth flagging directly rather than burying in the plan file:

**The referral-vs-job-board "tie" was an artifact, not a finding.** 2 of the 6 duplicate-candidate pairs span Job Board and Referral for the same physical person, and in both cases the Job Board application was rejected while the Referral application got hired. That's 40% of the counted "referral hires" sitting on identity confusion. Deduped with first-touch attribution, Job Board jumps to 33.3% of hires (clear leader, not a tie) — the efficiency gap (Job Board converts far worse per-candidate) survives, but the exact "tied at 26.9%" claim doesn't.

**Both offer-acceptance numbers are noisier than they look.** Wilson 95% CIs for 72.2% (Pending=fail) and 83.9% (Pending excluded) are [56%, 84%] and [67%, 93%] — they overlap. At only 36 offers, the "12-point definitional swing" I flagged isn't even statistically distinguishable from noise. That's now a first-class D3 requirement: show the rate with its n and interval, never a bare percentage.

I also checked department-funnel granularity (single-digit cells at full stage detail — needs coarser buckets) and right-censoring (30% of applications are still open, concentrated in the last 3 months — any recency trend needs those months excluded or it'll look artificially worse than it is).

The plan now has a dedicated "Correctness re-check" section up top with all of this, the cross-cut catalog is tiered by actual statistical power (Tier 1 decision-grade vs Tier 2 exploratory) instead of listed flat, and the roadmap section notes this sharpens candidate H into a real instrumentation build (CI-aware, censoring-aware) rather than "just wire up a number."

Did you think about people dropping off mid-interviews or not attending interviews, like ghosting us? Have you thought about that? Maybe that might be another reason, so that view or that data search can further make us think about the product better. This is one example of what I was thinking about. Also, as an idea, I was very confused about how to understand how many rounds a particular candidate took. Did it take 1 round, or did it take 3 rounds? For each round, what was the feedback? Did he pass the round, or did he not pass the round for every interview? Basically, the data structure itself, I was confused about whether there is some way to understand the different interview rounds taken by one single candidate, the stages, and the feedback, etc., between those rounds. That was one thought I had. Also, different tables say similar things but in different ways:

* One table says whether a person has completed or not.

## Interview-journey structure & ghosting — checked, here's the actual answer

You asked two concrete questions — can we tell how many rounds a candidate took and what
happened at each, and can we tell whether people are ghosting us mid-process. Checked both
directly against every record rather than assuming the schema supports it:

**How many rounds does a candidate actually take, per the data:**
- Only 143 of 350 applications (41%) have *any* interview logged at all. Of those, 126 have
  exactly 1 interview and 17 have exactly 2 — **nobody in this dataset has 3 or more logged
  interviews**, even though `Round` has 5 distinct values (Screen, Technical 1, Technical 2,
  Bar Raiser, Hiring Manager) that imply a longer process exists conceptually.
- **58% of Rejected applications (116/200) have zero interviews at all** — they were
  screened out before ever reaching an interview. Only 42% of rejections (84/200) happened
  after at least one interview. This matters directly for the job-board question: if Job
  Board's volume is mostly getting filtered at the resume/screen stage rather than the
  interview stage, that's a different (and cheaper) problem than a "the interview process
  itself doesn't work for this channel" story — this is now cross-cut #22 below, sharpened.
- Even Hired applications mostly show only 1 interview (23/26 = 88%) — a real single-round
  hiring model is possible, but combined with the round-sequence finding below, this reads
  more like sparse/synthetic interview logging than a genuine one-round process.
- **The `Round` field does not follow a consistent sequence.** Where 2 interviews exist on
  one application, the pairings are inconsistent — (Screen, Bar Raiser) skips both Technical
  rounds; (Technical 1, Hiring Manager) skips Bar Raiser; 63 applications have *only* a
  "Technical 1" round logged with no Screen before it. There's no canonical funnel order
  being followed. So a "candidate journey" view is buildable (join Interviews→Application,
  sort by Scheduled On) and worth having, but it will show short, irregularly-ordered
  journeys, not the clean 3-5 stage funnel the Round field's own value list implies — that
  irregularity is itself a D4 finding, not a bug in how I'd build the view.
- There's also no explicit "passed this round" flag anywhere — `Recommendation` is the
  interviewer's opinion (Hire/No Hire/Strong Hire/Strong No Hire), not a gate. Whether a
  candidate "passed" has to be inferred from whether the application's Stage advanced after
  that interview — which is itself only as reliable as Stage is (see the sync-lag finding
  below), so the journey view needs to carry both the interview verdict *and* the
  subsequent Stage/Status, and let the reader see where they diverge rather than asserting
  a clean pass/fail per round.

**Ghosting / no-shows — the magnitude is real, the attribution isn't there:**
- 10 No Show + 7 Cancelled + 5 Rescheduled = 22/160 interviews (13.75%) didn't complete as
  scheduled — that count is solid.
- But **who caused it is not recoverable from this schema**: there's no "cancelled by"
  field, and for the 22 non-completed interviews, `Feedback` is populated for only 4 of
  them, `Completed On` for only 4, `Score` for only 4 — the rest are bare records with no
  supporting detail. I can report the 13.75% figure and flag it as an operational-efficiency
  finding, but I cannot honestly split it into "candidate ghosted us" vs "we rescheduled/
  cancelled on them" without either reading the 4 free-text Feedback notes that do exist (too
  thin to generalize from) or asking Acme for a field that doesn't currently exist. This is a
  genuine data-gap to name plainly in D4, not something to approximate past.

## Schema concept ledger — is anything actually duplicated, or does it just look that way?

Going through every "status-like" field across the schema, what it actually represents, and
whether it's redundant with another one — rather than assuming column count itself is the
problem:

| Field | Represents | Redundant with another field? | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Interviews.Outcome` (Completed/No Show/Cancelled/Rescheduled) | Did the interview *event* happen as scheduled — logistics, not judgment | No — nothing else captures this | Keep |
| `Interviews.Recommendation` (Hire/No Hire/Strong Hire/Strong No Hire) | One interviewer's subjective verdict for one round | No — distinct axis from Outcome (an interview can complete and still get "No Hire") | Keep |
| `Applications.Stage` (Applied/Screening/Interview/Offer/Hired/Rejected/Withdrawn) | Current pipeline phase | Overlaps with `Status`, but not fully — see below | Keep as the primary field |
| `Applications.Status` (Active/Closed) | Coarse "is this decided yet" | **Partially** — should be a pure function of Stage (Active iff Stage not in {Hired,Rejected,Withdrawn}) but isn't always: the 10 Offer-stage applications split into 5×(Active, Offer still Pending) and 5×(Closed, Offer Declined) — Status is quietly tracking the linked Offer's resolution even when Stage fails to. | This is the real redundancy, and it's the wrong kind — a field that's *supposed to* be derived but is hand-maintained separately, so it can (and did) drift from Stage. Don't delete either field; make Status (and Stage's Hired/Rejected transitions) a computed rollup from Interviews/Offers events instead of two independently-settable fields. This is the actual fix behind candidate A in the roadmap list — not "sync a bug," but "stop hand-maintaining a field that should be a formula." |
| `Offers.Status` (Pending/Accepted/Declined) | The offer's own lifecycle — a distinct real-world object | No — Applications.Stage should be *downstream* of this, not a parallel record of it | Keep; make it the single source of truth Applications.Stage/Status derive from |
| `Job Openings.Status` (Open/Filled/On Hold/Cancelled) | The requisition's own lifecycle — a different real-world object (the job, not the candidate) | No | Keep — same field *name* as Applications/Offers.Status is a naming coincidence, not the same concept; always qualify by table when joining |

**Bottom line on "too many columns":** none of these are pure duplicates once you name what
each one actually represents — collapsing them would lose information (an interview can
complete with a bad recommendation; an offer can be declined while the application record
lags behind). The real problem isn't column *count*, it's that `Applications.Status` is
manually settable when it should be computed — that's a narrower, more useful fix than "fewer
columns," and it's exactly the mechanism behind the Stage/Status lag bug found earlier.

+  interviewer's opinion (Hire/No Hire/Strong Hire/Strong No Hire), not a gate. Whether a
+  candidate "passed" has to be inferred from whether the application's Stage advanced after
+  that interview — which is itself only as reliable as Stage is (see the sync-lag finding
+  below), so the journey view needs to carry both the interview verdict *and* the
+  subsequent Stage/Status, and let the reader see where they diverge rather than asserting
+  a clean pass/fail per round.
+**Ghosting / no-shows — the magnitude is real, the attribution isn't there:**
+- 10 No Show + 7 Cancelled + 5 Rescheduled = 22/160 interviews (13.75%) didn't complete as
+  scheduled — that count is solid.
+- But **who caused it is not recoverable from this schema**: there's no "cancelled by"
+  field, and for the 22 non-completed interviews, `Feedback` is populated for only 4 of
+  them, `Completed On` for only 4, `Score` for only 4 — the rest are bare records with no
+  supporting detail. I can report the 13.75% figure and flag it as an operational-efficiency
+  finding, but I cannot honestly split it into "candidate ghosted us" vs "we rescheduled/
+  cancelled on them" without either reading the 4 free-text Feedback notes that do exist (too
+  thin to generalize from) or asking Acme for a field that doesn't currently exist. This is a
+  genuine data-gap to name plainly in D4, not something to approximate past.
+## Schema concept ledger — is anything actually duplicated, or does it just look that way?
+Going through every "status-like" field across the schema, what it actually represents, and
+whether it's redundant with another one — rather than assuming column count itself is the
+problem:
+| Field | Represents | Redundant with another field? | Recommendation |
+| `Interviews.Outcome` (Completed/No Show/Cancelled/Rescheduled) | Did the interview *event* happen as scheduled — logistics, not judgment | No — nothing else captures this | Keep |

+| `Interviews.Recommendation` (Hire/No Hire/Strong Hire/Strong No Hire) | One interviewer's subjective verdict for one round | No — distinct axis from Outcome (an interview can complete and still get "No Hire") | Keep |
+| `Applications.Stage` (Applied/Screening/Interview/Offer/Hired/Rejected/Withdrawn) | Current pipeline phase | Overlaps with `Status`, but not fully — see below | Keep as the primary field |

+| `Applications.Status` (Active/Closed) | Coarse "is this decided yet" | **Partially** — should be a pure function of Stage (Active iff Stage not in {Hired,Rejected,Withdrawn}) but isn't always: the 10 Offer-stage applications split into 5×(Active, Offer still Pending) and 5×(Closed, Offer Declined) — Status is quietly tracking the linked Offer's resolution even when Stage fails to. | This is the real redundancy, and it's the wrong kind — a field that's *supposed to* be derived but is hand-maintained separately, so it can (and did) drift from Stage. Don't delete either field; make Status (and Stage's Hired/Rejected transitions) a computed rollup from Interviews/Offers events instead of two independently-settable fields. This is the actual fix behind candidate A in the roadmap list — not "sync a bug," but "stop hand-maintaining a field that should be a formula." |

+| `Offers.Status` (Pending/Accepted/Declined) | The offer's own lifecycle — a distinct real-world object | No — Applications.Stage should be *downstream* of this, not a parallel record of it | Keep; make it the single source of truth Applications.Stage/Status derive from |

+| `Job Openings.Status` (Open/Filled/On Hold/Cancelled) | The requisition's own lifecycle — a different real-world object (the job, not the candidate) | No | Keep — same field *name* as Applications/Offers.Status is a naming coincidence, not the same concept; always qualify by table when joining |
+**Bottom line on "too many columns":** none of these are pure duplicates once you name what
+each one actually represents — collapsing them would lose information (an interview can
+complete with a bad recommendation; an offer can be declined while the application record
+lags behind). The real problem isn't column *count*, it's that `Applications.Status` is
+manually settable when it should be computed — that's a narrower, more useful fix than "fewer
+columns," and it's exactly the mechanism behind the Stage/Status lag bug found earlier.

content.text:
Verified both against every record before writing them in:

**Interview rounds** — nobody in this dataset has 3+ logged interviews (max is 2, and 126 of 143 interviewed applications have just 1). 58% of all rejections (116/200) never had an interview at all — pure resume/screen rejects. And where 2 rounds exist, they don't follow a consistent order (Screen→Bar Raiser skipping both Technical rounds, 63 applications going straight to "Technical 1" with no Screen logged first) — the `Round` field isn't tracking a real sequential process. A candidate-journey view is buildable and worth having, but it'll show short, irregular journeys, not the clean funnel the field names imply — that irregularity is itself a finding, not something to smooth over.

**Ghosting** — the 13.75% no-show/cancel/reschedule rate is solid, but attribution isn't recoverable: no "cancelled-by" field exists, and 18 of 22 non-completed interviews have zero supporting detail (no feedback, no completed date, no score). I can report the magnitude, not who caused it — named as a real data gap rather than approximated.

**On the repeated status columns** — built a concept ledger (in the plan) walking through every status-like field. Most aren't actually redundant once you name what each represents (Outcome=logistics, Recommendation=one interviewer's opinion, Job Opening Status=a different real-world object entirely). The one genuine problem: `Applications.Status` should be a pure computed function of `Stage`, but isn't — it's hand-maintained separately and that's exactly why it drifted (the 5 declined-offer apps stuck at Stage=Offer). The fix isn't fewer columns, it's making Stage/Status a derived rollup instead of two independently-settable fields.

**On execution** — dropped the agent-fan-out idea per your note. Plan now commits to two plain scripts: `build_all_views.py` (deterministic, computes every cross-cut once, writes CSVs) and `challenge_all_views.py` (recomputes each number a second, differently-coded way and asserts they match — the challenger, done as code, not a model re-reading its own output). I'd run both once and work from their output files rather than re-deriving numbers interactively.

Also added an explicit impact-vs-effort prioritization rule to Step 4 so the final 6-week list doesn't pad out to "4 small items" when 2 bigger, better-evidenced ones would do more.
