input.plan:
# TalentFlow Q3 Roadmap — Analysis Plan

## Context

This is a 2-hour PM take-home: use Claude Code + the Airtable REST API to turn Acme's
real recruiting-ops data into a defensible Q3 roadmap. The VP of People has made two
claims by email (job boards drive 26.9% of hires and deserve accelerated integration
work; offer acceptance is ~72% and needs to move) and wants 6 engineer-weeks allocated
against them. Five deliverables are scored, D4 (data trust, 30 pts) weighted higher
than D2 (the roadmap itself, 20 pts) — the brief is explicitly rewarding skepticism
over a polished plan.

All 8 tables are already pulled locally (`talentflow/data/*.json`, 892 records) and a
browsable version is published. This plan documents what the data deep-dive already
found and lays out the specific follow-up checks needed before I write the five
deliverables — it does not draft the deliverables themselves yet.

## Correctness re-check — running this as a proficient analyst would, not a spreadsheet pass

You were right to push back. I went back through the headline numbers the way a rigorous
analyst actually should, before touching the bigger cross-cut catalog — and it changed two
of them. Recording what changed and why, plus the standing checks this means every cut
below has to pass, not just the two VP claims.

**1. The referral-vs-job-board finding was contaminated by the duplicate-candidate issue —
not just adjacent to it.** Of the 6 duplicate-phone candidate pairs, 2 span Job Board and
Referral for the *same physical person* — and in both cases, that person's Job Board
application was rejected and their Referral application was the one that got hired (Varun
Sharma: Job Board rejected 2025-04-08, Referral hired 2026-06-07; Aarav Menon: Referral
hired 2026-04-14, Job Board rejected 2026-05-30, opposite order). That means 2 of the 5
candidate-level Referral hires (40% of them) are people who also have a Job Board record —
the "referral converts 8x better" finding was standing partly on identity confusion, not
just noise. I re-ran it with the duplicates merged (first-touch attribution — the source of
whichever record was created earliest for that person):

| View | Job Board share of hires | Job Board candidate-conversion | Referral share of hires | Referral candidate-conversion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Raw (as recorded, hired-touch) | 26.9% (tied w/ Referral) | 3.7% | 26.9% (tied w/ Job Board) | 62.5% |
| Deduped, first-touch attribution | **33.3%** (clear largest) | 4.3% | 16.7% | 57.1% |

Attribution methodology (first-touch vs "credit whichever record actually converted") is a
real, named choice here, not a bug to resolve — first-touch is the standard marketing-
attribution convention and I'd default to it, but it needs to be stated as an assumption in
D1, not hidden. **What holds up under both views: Job Board is the volume leader and converts
far worse per-candidate than Referral, in both raw and deduped numbers.** What does *not*
hold up: the specific claim that the two channels are tied at 26.9% of hires — that tie was
an artifact of counting the same person under two source labels; deduped, Job Board is
unambiguously ahead on hire share. This changes the D1 verdict language: it's not "the VP's
'wide margin' claim is false," it's "the VP's *volume* framing is directionally fine, the
*efficiency* framing is the real story, and the exact 26.9% figure isn't robust to how you
resolve 12 duplicate records."

**2. Both headline rates are noisier than their point estimates suggest — checked with
Wilson confidence intervals, not just the raw percentage:**

| Number | Point estimate | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| Offer acceptance, Pending=fail | 72.2% (26/36) | **[56.0%, 84.2%]** |
| Offer acceptance, Pending excluded | 83.9% (26/31) | **[67.4%, 92.9%]** |
| Job Board candidate-conversion | 3.7% (7/191) | [1.8%, 7.4%] |
| Referral candidate-conversion (raw) | 62.5% (5/8) | **[30.6%, 86.3%]** |

The two offer-acceptance CIs **overlap** (56-84% vs 67-93%, overlapping 67-84%) — at n=36
offers, the "12-point swing from one definitional choice" I flagged earlier is not
statistically distinguishable from sampling noise. That doesn't make the definitional
question unimportant (D3 still needs one canonical rule), but it means neither 72.2% nor
83.9% should be presented to the VP as a precise numeryou'd bet the plan on — this is the
single most important thing to say about Claim 2, and it belongs in D3's "what the
dashboard shows when the answer is ambiguous" requirement directly: **show the rate with its
n and interval, never a bare percentage, given how few offers there are.**
Referral's conversion-rate CI is enormous ([30.6%, 86.3%]) because n=8 — Job Board being much
worse is solid (the CIs don't come close to overlapping), but the *exact size* of Referral's
advantage is not something 8 data points can tell you. Directionally real, precisely
unknowable — say both parts.

**3. Department-level funnels will be underpowered at full stage granularity.** Applications
per department range from 23 (Finance) to 69 (Sales) across 7 Stage values — that's 3 to 10
per stage per department on average, most cells in single digits before any second dimension
(source, level) is added. Any department × stage cross-cut needs to collapse to 3-4 coarse
buckets (e.g. Active-early / Active-late / Hired / Rejected+Withdrawn) rather than the full
7-value Stage field, or it will report noise as pattern. This changes how cross-cuts #1, #3,
#4, #7 in the catalog below need to be built, not whether to build them.

**4. Right-censoring: 105 of 350 applications (30%) are still open (`Status = Active`), and
they're heavily concentrated in the most recent months** — 23 opened in June 2026 alone, 13
in July, 9 in August, vs. single digits per month before 2026-04. Any month-over-month trend
in hire rate or acceptance rate will look mechanically worse for recent months purely because
those cohorts haven't finished flowing through the pipeline yet, not because anything
actually got worse. This directly matters for cross-cut #20 (monthly trend) and for reading
the VP's own "the board is asking about it, it needs moving" framing — if the VP is looking
at a recent-quarter snapshot, part of what they're seeing may be pipeline lag, not a real
decline. The fix: exclude the most recent 2-3 months from any trend claim (cohorts need time
to mature/resolve), or use time-to-event framing instead of a point-in-time rate. This needs
to be checked *before* claiming the rate has moved at all — which is possible the VP hasn't
done either.

**Standing rules this sets for every cross-cut in the catalog below** (not just the two VP
claims): (a) report every rate with its n and a Wilson CI, never a bare percentage; (b) check
expected cell size before running any 2+ dimension cut, and collapse categories rather than
report single-digit cells as if they were signal; (c) test source/channel-based findings
against both raw and duplicate-resolved candidate identity, the way Claim 1 just was; (d)
exclude or clearly flag any time-based cut's most recent 2-3 months for right-censoring.

## Interview-journey structure & ghosting — checked, here's the actual answer

You asked two concrete questions — can we tell how many rounds a candidate took and what
happened at each, and can we tell whether people are ghosting us mid-process. Checked both
directly against every record rather than assuming the schema supports it:

**How many rounds does a candidate actually take, per the data:**
- Only 143 of 350 applications (41%) have *any* interview logged at all. Of those, 126 have
  exactly 1 interview and 17 have exactly 2 — **nobody in this dataset has 3 or more logged
  interviews**, even though `Round` has 5 distinct values (Screen, Technical 1, Technical 2,
  Bar Raiser, Hiring Manager) that imply a longer process exists conceptually.
- **58% of Rejected applications (116/200) have zero interviews at all** — they were
  screened out before ever reaching an interview. Only 42% of rejections (84/200) happened
  after at least one interview. This matters directly for the job-board question: if Job
  Board's volume is mostly getting filtered at the resume/screen stage rather than the
  interview stage, that's a different (and cheaper) problem than a "the interview process
  itself doesn't work for this channel" story — this is now cross-cut #22 below, sharpened.
- Even Hired applications mostly show only 1 interview (23/26 = 88%) — a real single-round
  hiring model is possible, but combined with the round-sequence finding below, this reads
  more like sparse/synthetic interview logging than a genuine one-round process.
- **The `Round` field does not follow a consistent sequence.** Where 2 interviews exist on
  one application, the pairings are inconsistent — (Screen, Bar Raiser) skips both Technical
  rounds; (Technical 1, Hiring Manager) skips Bar Raiser; 63 applications have *only* a
  "Technical 1" round logged with no Screen before it. There's no canonical funnel order
  being followed. So a "candidate journey" view is buildable (join Interviews→Application,
  sort by Scheduled On) and worth having, but it will show short, irregularly-ordered
  journeys, not the clean 3-5 stage funnel the Round field's own value list implies — that
  irregularity is itself a D4 finding, not a bug in how I'd build the view.
- There's also no explicit "passed this round" flag anywhere — `Recommendation` is the
  interviewer's opinion (Hire/No Hire/Strong Hire/Strong No Hire), not a gate. Whether a
  candidate "passed" has to be inferred from whether the application's Stage advanced after
  that interview — which is itself only as reliable as Stage is (see the sync-lag finding
  below), so the journey view needs to carry both the interview verdict *and* the
  subsequent Stage/Status, and let the reader see where they diverge rather than asserting
  a clean pass/fail per round.

**Ghosting / no-shows — the magnitude is real, the attribution isn't there:**
- 10 No Show + 7 Cancelled + 5 Rescheduled = 22/160 interviews (13.75%) didn't complete as
  scheduled — that count is solid.
- But **who caused it is not recoverable from this schema**: there's no "cancelled by"
  field, and for the 22 non-completed interviews, `Feedback` is populated for only 4 of
  them, `Completed On` for only 4, `Score` for only 4 — the rest are bare records with no
  supporting detail. I can report the 13.75% figure and flag it as an operational-efficiency
  finding, but I cannot honestly split it into "candidate ghosted us" vs "we rescheduled/
  cancelled on them" without either reading the 4 free-text Feedback notes that do exist (too
  thin to generalize from) or asking Acme for a field that doesn't currently exist. This is a
  genuine data-gap to name plainly in D4, not something to approximate past.

## Schema concept ledger — is anything actually duplicated, or does it just look that way?

Going through every "status-like" field across the schema, what it actually represents, and
whether it's redundant with another one — rather than assuming column count itself is the
problem:

| Field | Represents | Redundant with another field? | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Interviews.Outcome` (Completed/No Show/Cancelled/Rescheduled) | Did the interview *event* happen as scheduled — logistics, not judgment | No — nothing else captures this | Keep |
| `Interviews.Recommendation` (Hire/No Hire/Strong Hire/Strong No Hire) | One interviewer's subjective verdict for one round | No — distinct axis from Outcome (an interview can complete and still get "No Hire") | Keep |
| `Applications.Stage` (Applied/Screening/Interview/Offer/Hired/Rejected/Withdrawn) | Current pipeline phase | Overlaps with `Status`, but not fully — see below | Keep as the primary field |
| `Applications.Status` (Active/Closed) | Coarse "is this decided yet" | **Partially** — should be a pure function of Stage (Active iff Stage not in {Hired,Rejected,Withdrawn}) but isn't always: the 10 Offer-stage applications split into 5×(Active, Offer still Pending) and 5×(Closed, Offer Declined) — Status is quietly tracking the linked Offer's resolution even when Stage fails to. | This is the real redundancy, and it's the wrong kind — a field that's *supposed to* be derived but is hand-maintained separately, so it can (and did) drift from Stage. Don't delete either field; make Status (and Stage's Hired/Rejected transitions) a computed rollup from Interviews/Offers events instead of two independently-settable fields. This is the actual fix behind candidate A in the roadmap list — not "sync a bug," but "stop hand-maintaining a field that should be a formula." |
| `Offers.Status` (Pending/Accepted/Declined) | The offer's own lifecycle — a distinct real-world object | No — Applications.Stage should be *downstream* of this, not a parallel record of it | Keep; make it the single source of truth Applications.Stage/Status derive from |
| `Job Openings.Status` (Open/Filled/On Hold/Cancelled) | The requisition's own lifecycle — a different real-world object (the job, not the candidate) | No | Keep — same field *name* as Applications/Offers.Status is a naming coincidence, not the same concept; always qualify by table when joining |

**Bottom line on "too many columns":** none of these are pure duplicates once you name what
each one actually represents — collapsing them would lose information (an interview can
complete with a bad recommendation; an offer can be declined while the application record
lags behind). The real problem isn't column *count*, it's that `Applications.Status` is
manually settable when it should be computed — that's a narrower, more useful fix than "fewer
columns," and it's exactly the mechanism behind the Stage/Status lag bug found earlier.

## Table interconnection audit — current state vs recommended state

You asked specifically about the Interviews→Interviewer / Applications link and whether
pointers between tables are actually synchronized. I checked this exhaustively (every
record, not a sample) rather than assuming. Two different things came back, and they
point in opposite directions:

**Current state, verified against all records: the links themselves are 100% intact.**
I checked every forward/reverse link pair Airtable exposes — Interviews.Interviewer ↔
People.Interviews, Interviews.Application ↔ Applications.Interviews, Applications.Recruiter
↔ People["Applications as Recruiter"], Applications.Candidate ↔ Candidates.Applications,
Applications.Opening ↔ JobOpenings.Applications, Offers.Application ↔ Applications.Offers,
JobOpenings.Department ↔ Departments["Job Openings"], People.Department ↔ Departments.People,
JobOpenings.Recruiter ↔ People["Reqs as Recruiter"], JobOpenings.HiringManager ↔
People["Reqs as Hiring Manager"] — **0 mismatches across all of them.** So if you searched
an Interview ID inside Applications.Interviews and it wasn't there, that's not what's
happening — the record-ID pointers are clean. Airtable maintains these automatically and
the data respects it everywhere.

**What's actually wrong — and it's a bigger finding than a broken pointer — is that the
*people assigned* to a given piece of work don't line up with each other's department at
all, system-wide, not just for interviewers:**

| Relationship checked | Same department | Different department | Mismatch rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interview's Interviewer vs the Opening being interviewed for | 22 | 138 | **86%** |
| Application's Recruiter vs the Opening's department | 80 | 270 | **77%** |
| Job Opening's Hiring Manager vs the Opening's own department | 3 | 21 | **87%** |
| Application's Recruiter vs that application's Interviewer (same app) | 0 same person, ever | 160 / 160 | **100%** — recruiter and interviewer are never the same person on any of the 160 interviews |

This is why you noticed it on Interviewer specifically — it's the most visible instance of
a pattern that runs through Recruiter and Hiring Manager assignment too. I also checked
whether this is just because there aren't enough people to go around: there are only 6
Interviewers / 4 Recruiters / 4 Hiring Managers for 8 departments, so *some* cross-department
assignment is structurally forced — but even departments that have their own dedicated
interviewer still get cross-department assignments most of the time, so scarcity doesn't
explain an 86% mismatch rate. Every person's Role field is also perfectly single-purpose
(a Recruiter never interviews, an Interviewer never recruits, 0 exceptions) — that plus the
random-looking department assignment reads like a data-generation artifact (roles and
department links were sampled independently of each other) rather than an organic
org chart. I'm flagging this as a trust caveat, not asserting certainty either way.

**Recommended state:** before any interviewer-, recruiter-, or hiring-manager-level cut is
used to justify a decision, this needs to be named explicitly: either (a) this is how Acme
actually staffs hiring — a floating interviewer/recruiter pool, not department-dedicated,
which is a legitimate model and just needs to be understood before drawing conclusions from
department-level people-cuts, or (b) it's a seeding/sync artifact in this specific export and
person-level cuts should be treated as low-confidence until confirmed with Acme. I can't tell
which from the data alone — this goes in D4 as an open question, not a resolved bug, and it
gates how much weight cross-cuts #14–16 below (interviewer calibration, cross-dept quality
impact) should carry.

**One more synchronization pattern worth surfacing while on this topic:** `Applications.Status`
is not simply derived from `Stage` — for the 10 applications sitting at `Stage = Offer`,
`Status` splits cleanly into 5×(Active, linked Offer=Pending) and 5×(Closed, linked
Offer=Declined) — Status tracks the *Offer* record's resolution faithfully even when Stage
itself fails to advance to Rejected. So `Status` is actually the more reliable "is this
decided" signal; `Stage`'s specific bucket (Hired vs Rejected) is what lags. That refines the
earlier D3-relevant finding: don't discard Stage/Status as broken, use Status for "is this
closed" and Offers.Status as ground truth for "closed how."

## Multi-table cross-cut plan — going past the two claims

Point taken that the current 6-week candidate list (A–H above) is a set of one-week fixes,
not big thinking. The two VP claims only required 2-3 tables joined one way. Getting to
sharper, more ambitious project ideas means actually multiplying the tables against each
other the way you described — funnel × department × source × level × time × people — before
guessing what to build. Below is the plan for that, not the execution.

**Step 0 — lock the identity/key model first, before any cross-cut, so nothing downstream
inherits an error:**
- Canonical join key everywhere is the Airtable record `id`, never a business string ID —
  already proven necessary (4 `Application ID` values are each reused by two unrelated
  records; joining on the string ID silently merges the wrong rows).
- Canonical **person** identity for Candidates is not yet decided. 6 of 300 candidate
  records (4%) are near-certain duplicates of the same physical person (identical phone +
  name, different email/record). Before any candidate-level (not application-level) funnel
  or source cut runs, I need to pick a merge rule (phone-normalized match, tie-broken by
  name) and produce both a raw view and a canonical-person view, so every cross-cut below
  can report "as recorded" and "as-deduped" side by side rather than silently picking one.
- People (14 rows) needs no dedup — checked, clean, one row per person, roles mutually
  exclusive.
- Schema redundancy check, so I don't build 20 tables on top of columns that are secretly
  the same thing: `Status` fields exist in three unrelated tables (Applications: Active/
  Closed; Job Openings: Open/Filled/On Hold/Cancelled; Offers: Pending/Accepted/Declined) —
  same column name, three different enumerations, not mergeable, just needs table-qualified
  naming so a cross-cut never accidentally groups by the wrong "Status." `Outcome` vs
  `Recommendation` on Interviews are genuinely different axes (process vs verdict) — keep
  both. No column found so far is pure duplication of another; will re-check once the
  Rejection Reason distribution (next steps #3) is in.

**Step 1 — the cross-cut catalog, tiered by statistical power, not just listed.** Given the
volumes involved (350 applications / 300 candidates / 160 interviews / 36 offers / 24
openings / 8 departments / 14 people), most 3-way splits are thin before they're even run —
the department-funnel granularity check above already proved that out. So every cut below
gets a tier, decided by expected cell size, not by how interesting it sounds:

- **Tier 1 — confirmatory, decision-grade:** n per cell is large enough (generally 20+) to
  report a point estimate with a usable CI and actually change a decision. These are the
  ones D1/D2/D3 can cite directly.
- **Tier 2 — exploratory, hypothesis-generating only:** cells will often be single digits.
  Still worth computing — this is where "creative, more ambitious idea" candidates for D2
  are most likely to come from — but every output carries its n and gets reported as
  directional, never as a decision-grade percentage on its own.

Each row below is one self-contained, deterministic computation (funnel counts + % drop +
median days between stages, where time applies), grouped by what it's meant to surface:

*Funnel × dimension × time*
1. **[Tier 1]** Source × Stage funnel + time-to-each-stage (n=350, largest categories are
   fine; small ones like Campus n=4 get reported as n-flagged only)
2. **[Tier 1, coarse buckets]** Department × Stage funnel — collapsed to 4 macro-stages
   (Active-early / Active-late / Hired / Rejected+Withdrawn) per the granularity check above,
   not the raw 7-value Stage
3. **[Tier 2]** Department × Source interaction — most department×source cells will be
   single-digit; usable only to spot an outlier worth a follow-up, not to size anything
4. **[Tier 1]** Level (Junior/Mid/Senior, from Job Openings.Level) × Stage funnel — need to
   check level cardinality/counts first, likely 3 buckets over 350 apps is workable
5. **[Tier 2]** Employment Type (Full-time/Part-time/Contract) × Stage funnel — likely
   dominated by one type; check the actual split before assuming this is usable at all
6. **[Tier 2]** Candidate City × Stage funnel — many distinct cities over 300 candidates,
   expect thin cells; only report cities with n≥20
7. **[Tier 1]** Recruiter × Stage funnel + workload-adjusted time-in-stage (only 4
   recruiters, each with 30-113 applications per the earlier People roster — well-powered)
8. **[Tier 1]** Interview Round × Outcome × Recommendation (n=160 interviews, 5 round types
   — workable)

*Candidate segment × offer outcome — all Tier 2, offers n=36 total*
9. Notice Period bucket × Level × Offer-Accept rate — flag explicitly: 36 offers split 3 ways
   will mostly be n<5 per cell; report as directional only, with n shown
10. Expected-vs-Current CTC gap bucket × Accept rate — same n=36 constraint
11. Offer Base CTC vs Salary Band position (below/within/above) × Accept rate — same
    constraint, but worth checking as a possible root cause even at low n
12. Years-experience bucket × Level applied-for — candidate-level (n=300) not offer-level,
    so this one can move to Tier 1 for the mis-leveling question itself, even though its
    downstream link to Accept rate stays Tier 2
13. Candidate City × Offer-Accept rate — Tier 2, n=36 offers across many cities

*Interviewer/quality lens — read together with the department-affinity caveat above; only
6 interviewers, so per-interviewer cuts are Tier 1 on volume but need the affinity caveat*
14. **[Tier 1, caveated]** Interviewer × avg Score × Recommendation mix × downstream Outcome
    (25-33 interviews per interviewer — enough n, but the assignment-affinity finding above
    means "interviewer effect" may be confounded with "which candidates get routed to them,"
    not a clean read on interviewer skill alone)
15. **[Tier 1]** Round × avg Score trend (n=160, 5 rounds — workable, do scores genuinely
    climb Screen→Technical→Bar Raiser or is an early round just noise overridden later?)
16. **[Tier 2]** Same-department vs cross-department interview assignment × avg Score/Outcome
    — the direct test of whether the affinity break above actually matters for quality;
    worth running even at modest n because the answer (matters / doesn't) changes how much
    weight #14 can carry

*Operational timing — Tier 1, application/interview counts support this*
17. Time-in-stage waterfall (Applied→Screened→Interview→Offer→Closed), department-level
    medians *and* the outlier tail — find the real bottleneck instead of assuming one
18. **[Tier 2 — only 24 openings]** Requisition aging: Opened On → Target Close → actual
    Filled date, by department/level; useful as a specific list of overdue reqs even if not
    statistically generalizable
19. Interview scheduling lead time (Applied On → First Interview On) and offer lead time
    (Final Interview On → Offered On), by department/source
20. **[Tier 1, with the right-censoring fix from the correctness re-check applied]** Monthly
    trend of applications, hires, and acceptance rate, excluding the most recent 2-3 months
    to avoid the pipeline-lag bias already found — this is the check for whether the VP's
    "it needs moving" alarm reflects a real trend or a censored recent snapshot

*Referral network — Tier 2, small base (8 candidates) but high-value if a pattern holds*
21. `Referred By` chains — who refers, how many of their referrals convert, is there a
    concentrated set of "super-referrers" worth building a program around (feeds directly
    into candidate E from the current list, with actual evidence behind the sizing, though
    n=8 referral candidates means this is a lead to validate with Acme, not a proof)
22. **[Tier 1]** Rejection Reason × Source × Department, **split by pre-interview vs
    post-interview rejection** (58% of all rejections happen with zero interviews logged —
    this cut needs to separate "never got an interview" from "interviewed and rejected"
    before asking whether Job Board's volume is a real pipeline or mostly resume-stage
    noise; conflating the two would understate how early Job Board applicants actually
    drop off)
23. **[Tier 2, structural output not just a stat]** Candidate/application interview-journey
    table: every application's interviews in order (Round, Outcome, Score, Recommendation)
    alongside the Stage/Status at the time — this is the direct answer to "how many rounds
    did this candidate take and what happened," built once as a reusable view rather than
    answered ad hoc; per the check above it will show mostly 1-2 round journeys with
    non-canonical round ordering, which the output should surface plainly rather than paper
    over
24. **[Tier 1]** No-show/cancellation rate (13.75%, n=160) by Department/Source/Round —
    the magnitude is reportable even though *attribution* (candidate vs company-caused)
    is not recoverable from this schema, as established above; this cut is descriptive
    only and must say so

**Step 2 — challenger pass on every cut, not just a spot-check on the two VP numbers.**
Same discipline that just caught the referral-attribution and Wilson-CI issues above,
applied systematically:
- Recompute the headline number a second, differently-coded way (e.g. pandas groupby vs a
  manual dict aggregation) — must match exactly before it's accepted.
- Every proportion gets a Wilson CI alongside the point estimate, reported together — not
  optional for Tier 1 cuts, and mandatory for any Tier 2 cut that makes it into a deliverable.
- Re-run every source/channel-based cut once on raw candidate identities and once on the
  deduped/canonical view from Step 0, and report the delta — if a conclusion flips between
  the two (like Claim 1's tie did), that conclusion is not usable as-is and gets flagged, not
  quietly resolved in whichever direction is more convenient.
- Any time-based cut gets the right-censoring check applied (exclude or flag the most recent
  2-3 months) before a trend is claimed.
- Any cell with n < 10 gets marked low-confidence explicitly, not silently dropped — "not
  enough data to say" is itself a usable answer and goes in the output.
- One adversarial sentence per surviving finding: "this could be wrong because ___" —
  before it goes in front of anyone.

**Step 3 — how I'd actually build this (once you approve), revised per your instruction to
spend no agent/model bandwidth on the arithmetic itself:** no Agent-tool fan-out for this —
that was more machinery than the problem needs, and it still risks a model summarizing
numbers instead of code computing them. Two plain scripts instead:

## Approved Plan:
# TalentFlow Q3 Roadmap — Analysis Plan

## Context

This is a 2-hour PM take-home: use Claude Code + the Airtable REST API to turn Acme's
real recruiting-ops data into a defensible Q3 roadmap. The VP of People has made two
claims by email (job boards drive 26.9% of hires and deserve accelerated integration
work; offer acceptance is ~72% and needs to move) and wants 6 engineer-weeks allocated
against them. Five deliverables are scored, D4 (data trust, 30 pts) weighted higher
than D2 (the roadmap itself, 20 pts) — the brief is explicitly rewarding skepticism
over a polished plan.

All 8 tables are already pulled locally (`talentflow/data/*.json`, 892 records) and a
browsable version is published. This plan documents what the data deep-dive already
found and lays out the specific follow-up checks needed before I write the five
deliverables — it does not draft the deliverables themselves yet.

## Correctness re-check — running this as a proficient analyst would, not a spreadsheet pass

You were right to push back. I went back through the headline numbers the way a rigorous
analyst actually should, before touching the bigger cross-cut catalog — and it changed two
of them. Recording what changed and why, plus the standing checks this means every cut
below has to pass, not just the two VP claims.

**1. The referral-vs-job-board finding was contaminated by the duplicate-candidate issue —
not just adjacent to it.** Of the 6 duplicate-phone candidate pairs, 2 span Job Board and
Referral for the *same physical person* — and in both cases, that person's Job Board
application was rejected and their Referral application was the one that got hired (Varun
Sharma: Job Board rejected 2025-04-08, Referral hired 2026-06-07; Aarav Menon: Referral
hired 2026-04-14, Job Board rejected 2026-05-30, opposite order). That means 2 of the 5
candidate-level Referral hires (40% of them) are people who also have a Job Board record —
the "referral converts 8x better" finding was standing partly on identity confusion, not
just noise. I re-ran it with the duplicates merged (first-touch attribution — the source of
whichever record was created earliest for that person):

| View | Job Board share of hires | Job Board candidate-conversion | Referral share of hires | Referral candidate-conversion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Raw (as recorded, hired-touch) | 26.9% (tied w/ Referral) | 3.7% | 26.9% (tied w/ Job Board) | 62.5% |
| Deduped, first-touch attribution | **33.3%** (clear largest) | 4.3% | 16.7% | 57.1% |

Attribution methodology (first-touch vs "credit whichever record actually converted") is a
real, named choice here, not a bug to resolve — first-touch is the standard marketing-
attribution convention and I'd default to it, but it needs to be stated as an assumption in
D1, not hidden. **What holds up under both views: Job Board is the volume leader and converts
far worse per-candidate than Referral, in both raw and deduped numbers.** What does *not*
hold up: the specific claim that the two channels are tied at 26.9% of hires — that tie was
an artifact of counting the same person under two source labels; deduped, Job Board is
unambiguously ahead on hire share. This changes the D1 verdict language: it's not "the VP's
'wide margin' claim is false," it's "the VP's *volume* framing is directionally fine, the
*efficiency* framing is the real story, and the exact 26.9% figure isn't robust to how you
resolve 12 duplicate records."

**2. Both headline rates are noisier than their point estimates suggest — checked with
Wilson confidence intervals, not just the raw percentage:**

| Number | Point estimate | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| Offer acceptance, Pending=fail | 72.2% (26/36) | **[56.0%, 84.2%]** |
| Offer acceptance, Pending excluded | 83.9% (26/31) | **[67.4%, 92.9%]** |
| Job Board candidate-conversion | 3.7% (7/191) | [1.8%, 7.4%] |
| Referral candidate-conversion (raw) | 62.5% (5/8) | **[30.6%, 86.3%]** |

The two offer-acceptance CIs **overlap** (56-84% vs 67-93%, overlapping 67-84%) — at n=36
offers, the "12-point swing from one definitional choice" I flagged earlier is not
statistically distinguishable from sampling noise. That doesn't make the definitional
question unimportant (D3 still needs one canonical rule), but it means neither 72.2% nor
83.9% should be presented to the VP as a precise numeryou'd bet the plan on — this is the
single most important thing to say about Claim 2, and it belongs in D3's "what the
dashboard shows when the answer is ambiguous" requirement directly: **show the rate with its
n and interval, never a bare percentage, given how few offers there are.**
Referral's conversion-rate CI is enormous ([30.6%, 86.3%]) because n=8 — Job Board being much
worse is solid (the CIs don't come close to overlapping), but the *exact size* of Referral's
advantage is not something 8 data points can tell you. Directionally real, precisely
unknowable — say both parts.

**3. Department-level funnels will be underpowered at full stage granularity.** Applications
per department range from 23 (Finance) to 69 (Sales) across 7 Stage values — that's 3 to 10
per stage per department on average, most cells in single digits before any second dimension
(source, level) is added. Any department × stage cross-cut needs to collapse to 3-4 coarse
buckets (e.g. Active-early / Active-late / Hired / Rejected+Withdrawn) rather than the full
7-value Stage field, or it will report noise as pattern. This changes how cross-cuts #1, #3,
#4, #7 in the catalog below need to be built, not whether to build them.

**4. Right-censoring: 105 of 350 applications (30%) are still open (`Status = Active`), and
they're heavily concentrated in the most recent months** — 23 opened in June 2026 alone, 13
in July, 9 in August, vs. single digits per month before 2026-04. Any month-over-month trend
in hire rate or acceptance rate will look mechanically worse for recent months purely because
those cohorts haven't finished flowing through the pipeline yet, not because anything
actually got worse. This directly matters for cross-cut #20 (monthly trend) and for reading
the VP's own "the board is asking about it, it needs moving" framing — if the VP is looking
at a recent-quarter snapshot, part of what they're seeing may be pipeline lag, not a real
decline. The fix: exclude the most recent 2-3 months from any trend claim (cohorts need time
to mature/resolve), or use time-to-event framing instead of a point-in-time rate. This needs
to be checked *before* claiming the rate has moved at all — which is possible the VP hasn't
done either.

**Standing rules this sets for every cross-cut in the catalog below** (not just the two VP
claims): (a) report every rate with its n and a Wilson CI, never a bare percentage; (b) check
expected cell size before running any 2+ dimension cut, and collapse categories rather than
report single-digit cells as if they were signal; (c) test source/channel-based findings
against both raw and duplicate-resolved candidate identity, the way Claim 1 just was; (d)
exclude or clearly flag any time-based cut's most recent 2-3 months for right-censoring.

## Interview-journey structure & ghosting — checked, here's the actual answer

You asked two concrete questions — can we tell how many rounds a candidate took and what
happened at each, and can we tell whether people are ghosting us mid-process. Checked both
directly against every record rather than assuming the schema supports it:

**How many rounds does a candidate actually take, per the data:**
- Only 143 of 350 applications (41%) have *any* interview logged at all. Of those, 126 have
  exactly 1 interview and 17 have exactly 2 — **nobody in this dataset has 3 or more logged
  interviews**, even though `Round` has 5 distinct values (Screen, Technical 1, Technical 2,
  Bar Raiser, Hiring Manager) that imply a longer process exists conceptually.
- **58% of Rejected applications (116/200) have zero interviews at all** — they were
  screened out before ever reaching an interview. Only 42% of rejections (84/200) happened
  after at least one interview. This matters directly for the job-board question: if Job
  Board's volume is mostly getting filtered at the resume/screen stage rather than the
  interview stage, that's a different (and cheaper) problem than a "the interview process
  itself doesn't work for this channel" story — this is now cross-cut #22 below, sharpened.
- Even Hired applications mostly show only 1 interview (23/26 = 88%) — a real single-round
  hiring model is possible, but combined with the round-sequence finding below, this reads
  more like sparse/synthetic interview logging than a genuine one-round process.
- **The `Round` field does not follow a consistent sequence.** Where 2 interviews exist on
  one application, the pairings are inconsistent — (Screen, Bar Raiser) skips both Technical
  rounds; (Technical 1, Hiring Manager) skips Bar Raiser; 63 applications have *only* a
  "Technical 1" round logged with no Screen before it. There's no canonical funnel order
  being followed. So a "candidate journey" view is buildable (join Interviews→Application,
  sort by Scheduled On) and worth having, but it will show short, irregularly-ordered
  journeys, not the clean 3-5 stage funnel the Round field's own value list implies — that
  irregularity is itself a D4 finding, not a bug in how I'd build the view.
- There's also no explicit "passed this round" flag anywhere — `Recommendation` is the
  interviewer's opinion (Hire/No Hire/Strong Hire/Strong No Hire), not a gate. Whether a
  candidate "passed" has to be inferred from whether the application's Stage advanced after
  that interview — which is itself only as reliable as Stage is (see the sync-lag finding
  below), so the journey view needs to carry both the interview verdict *and* the
  subsequent Stage/Status, and let the reader see where they diverge rather than asserting
  a clean pass/fail per round.

**Ghosting / no-shows — the magnitude is real, the attribution isn't there:**
- 10 No Show + 7 Cancelled + 5 Rescheduled = 22/160 interviews (13.75%) didn't complete as
  scheduled — that count is solid.
- But **who caused it is not recoverable from this schema**: there's no "cancelled by"
  field, and for the 22 non-completed interviews, `Feedback` is populated for only 4 of
  them, `Completed On` for only 4, `Score` for only 4 — the rest are bare records with no
  supporting detail. I can report the 13.75% figure and flag it as an operational-efficiency
  finding, but I cannot honestly split it into "candidate ghosted us" vs "we rescheduled/
  cancelled on them" without either reading the 4 free-text Feedback notes that do exist (too
  thin to generalize from) or asking Acme for a field that doesn't currently exist. This is a
  genuine data-gap to name plainly in D4, not something to approximate past.

## Schema concept ledger — is anything actually duplicated, or does it just look that way?

Going through every "status-like" field across the schema, what it actually represents, and
whether it's redundant with another one — rather than assuming column count itself is the
problem:

| Field | Represents | Redundant with another field? | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Interviews.Outcome` (Completed/No Show/Cancelled/Rescheduled) | Did the interview *event* happen as scheduled — logistics, not judgment | No — nothing else captures this | Keep |
| `Interviews.Recommendation` (Hire/No Hire/Strong Hire/Strong No Hire) | One interviewer's subjective verdict for one round | No — distinct axis from Outcome (an interview can complete and still get "No Hire") | Keep |
| `Applications.Stage` (Applied/Screening/Interview/Offer/Hired/Rejected/Withdrawn) | Current pipeline phase | Overlaps with `Status`, but not fully — see below | Keep as the primary field |
| `Applications.Status` (Active/Closed) | Coarse "is this decided yet" | **Partially** — should be a pure function of Stage (Active iff Stage not in {Hired,Rejected,Withdrawn}) but isn't always: the 10 Offer-stage applications split into 5×(Active, Offer still Pending) and 5×(Closed, Offer Declined) — Status is quietly tracking the linked Offer's resolution even when Stage fails to. | This is the real redundancy, and it's the wrong kind — a field that's *supposed to* be derived but is hand-maintained separately, so it can (and did) drift from Stage. Don't delete either field; make Status (and Stage's Hired/Rejected transitions) a computed rollup from Interviews/Offers events instead of two independently-settable fields. This is the actual fix behind candidate A in the roadmap list — not "sync a bug," but "stop hand-maintaining a field that should be a formula." |
| `Offers.Status` (Pending/Accepted/Declined) | The offer's own lifecycle — a distinct real-world object | No — Applications.Stage should be *downstream* of this, not a parallel record of it | Keep; make it the single source of truth Applications.Stage/Status derive from |
| `Job Openings.Status` (Open/Filled/On Hold/Cancelled) | The requisition's own lifecycle — a different real-world object (the job, not the candidate) | No | Keep — same field *name* as Applications/Offers.Status is a naming coincidence, not the same concept; always qualify by table when joining |

**Bottom line on "too many columns":** none of these are pure duplicates once you name what
each one actually represents — collapsing them would lose information (an interview can
complete with a bad recommendation; an offer can be declined while the application record
lags behind). The real problem isn't column *count*, it's that `Applications.Status` is
manually settable when it should be computed — that's a narrower, more useful fix than "fewer
columns," and it's exactly the mechanism behind the Stage/Status lag bug found earlier.

## Table interconnection audit — current state vs recommended state

You asked specifically about the Interviews→Interviewer / Applications link and whether
pointers between tables are actually synchronized. I checked this exhaustively (every
record, not a sample) rather than assuming. Two different things came back, and they
point in opposite directions:

**Current state, verified against all records: the links themselves are 100% intact.**
I checked every forward/reverse link pair Airtable exposes — Interviews.Interviewer ↔
People.Interviews, Interviews.Application ↔ Applications.Interviews, Applications.Recruiter
↔ People["Applications as Recruiter"], Applications.Candidate ↔ Candidates.Applications,
Applications.Opening ↔ JobOpenings.Applications, Offers.Application ↔ Applications.Offers,
JobOpenings.Department ↔ Departments["Job Openings"], People.Department ↔ Departments.People,
JobOpenings.Recruiter ↔ People["Reqs as Recruiter"], JobOpenings.HiringManager ↔
People["Reqs as Hiring Manager"] — **0 mismatches across all of them.** So if you searched
an Interview ID inside Applications.Interviews and it wasn't there, that's not what's
happening — the record-ID pointers are clean. Airtable maintains these automatically and
the data respects it everywhere.

**What's actually wrong — and it's a bigger finding than a broken pointer — is that the
*people assigned* to a given piece of work don't line up with each other's department at
all, system-wide, not just for interviewers:**

| Relationship checked | Same department | Different department | Mismatch rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interview's Interviewer vs the Opening being interviewed for | 22 | 138 | **86%** |
| Application's Recruiter vs the Opening's department | 80 | 270 | **77%** |
| Job Opening's Hiring Manager vs the Opening's own department | 3 | 21 | **87%** |
| Application's Recruiter vs that application's Interviewer (same app) | 0 same person, ever | 160 / 160 | **100%** — recruiter and interviewer are never the same person on any of the 160 interviews |

This is why you noticed it on Interviewer specifically — it's the most visible instance of
a pattern that runs through Recruiter and Hiring Manager assignment too. I also checked
whether this is just because there aren't enough people to go around: there are only 6
Interviewers / 4 Recruiters / 4 Hiring Managers for 8 departments, so *some* cross-department
assignment is structurally forced — but even departments that have their own dedicated
interviewer still get cross-department assignments most of the time, so scarcity doesn't
explain an 86% mismatch rate. Every person's Role field is also perfectly single-purpose
(a Recruiter never interviews, an Interviewer never recruits, 0 exceptions) — that plus the
random-looking department assignment reads like a data-generation artifact (roles and
department links were sampled independently of each other) rather than an organic
org chart. I'm flagging this as a trust caveat, not asserting certainty either way.

**Recommended state:** before any interviewer-, recruiter-, or hiring-manager-level cut is
used to justify a decision, this needs to be named explicitly: either (a) this is how Acme
actually staffs hiring — a floating interviewer/recruiter pool, not department-dedicated,
which is a legitimate model and just needs to be understood before drawing conclusions from
department-level people-cuts, or (b) it's a seeding/sync artifact in this specific export and
person-level cuts should be treated as low-confidence until confirmed with Acme. I can't tell
which from the data alone — this goes in D4 as an open question, not a resolved bug, and it
gates how much weight cross-cuts #14–16 below (interviewer calibration, cross-dept quality
impact) should carry.

**One more synchronization pattern worth surfacing while on this topic:** `Applications.Status`
is not simply derived from `Stage` — for the 10 applications sitting at `Stage = Offer`,
`Status` splits cleanly into 5×(Active, linked Offer=Pending) and 5×(Closed, linked
Offer=Declined) — Status tracks the *Offer* record's resolution faithfully even when Stage
itself fails to advance to Rejected. So `Status` is actually the more reliable "is this
decided" signal; `Stage`'s specific bucket (Hired vs Rejected) is what lags. That refines the
earlier D3-relevant finding: don't discard Stage/Status as broken, use Status for "is this
closed" and Offers.Status as ground truth for "closed how."

## Multi-table cross-cut plan — going past the two claims

Point taken that the current 6-week candidate list (A–H above) is a set of one-week fixes,
not big thinking. The two VP claims only required 2-3 tables joined one way. Getting to
sharper, more ambitious project ideas means actually multiplying the tables against each
other the way you described — funnel × department × source × level × time × people — before
guessing what to build. Below is the plan for that, not the execution.

**Step 0 — lock the identity/key model first, before any cross-cut, so nothing downstream
inherits an error:**
- Canonical join key everywhere is the Airtable record `id`, never a business string ID —
  already proven necessary (4 `Application ID` values are each reused by two unrelated
  records; joining on the string ID silently merges the wrong rows).
- Canonical **person** identity for Candidates is not yet decided. 6 of 300 candidate
  records (4%) are near-certain duplicates of the same physical person (identical phone +
  name, different email/record). Before any candidate-level (not application-level) funnel
  or source cut runs, I need to pick a merge rule (phone-normalized match, tie-broken by
  name) and produce both a raw view and a canonical-person view, so every cross-cut below
  can report "as recorded" and "as-deduped" side by side rather than silently picking one.
- People (14 rows) needs no dedup — checked, clean, one row per person, roles mutually
  exclusive.
- Schema redundancy check, so I don't build 20 tables on top of columns that are secretly
  the same thing: `Status` fields exist in three unrelated tables (Applications: Active/
  Closed; Job Openings: Open/Filled/On Hold/Cancelled; Offers: Pending/Accepted/Declined) —
  same column name, three different enumerations, not mergeable, just needs table-qualified
  naming so a cross-cut never accidentally groups by the wrong "Status." `Outcome` vs
  `Recommendation` on Interviews are genuinely different axes (process vs verdict) — keep
  both. No column found so far is pure duplication of another; will re-check once the
  Rejection Reason distribution (next steps #3) is in.

**Step 1 — the cross-cut catalog, tiered by statistical power, not just listed.** Given the
volumes involved (350 applications / 300 candidates / 160 interviews / 36 offers / 24
openings / 8 departments / 14 people), most 3-way splits are thin before they're even run —
the department-funnel granularity check above already proved that out. So every cut below
gets a tier, decided by expected cell size, not by how interesting it sounds:

- **Tier 1 — confirmatory, decision-grade:** n per cell is large enough (generally 20+) to
  report a point estimate with a usable CI and actually change a decision. These are the
  ones D1/D2/D3 can cite directly.
- **Tier 2 — exploratory, hypothesis-generating only:** cells will often be single digits.
  Still worth computing — this is where "creative, more ambitious idea" candidates for D2
  are most likely to come from — but every output carries its n and gets reported as
  directional, never as a decision-grade percentage on its own.

Each row below is one self-contained, deterministic computation (funnel counts + % drop +
median days between stages, where time applies), grouped by what it's meant to surface:

*Funnel × dimension × time*
1. **[Tier 1]** Source × Stage funnel + time-to-each-stage (n=350, largest categories are
   fine; small ones like Campus n=4 get reported as n-flagged only)
2. **[Tier 1, coarse buckets]** Department × Stage funnel — collapsed to 4 macro-stages
   (Active-early / Active-late / Hired / Rejected+Withdrawn) per the granularity check above,
   not the raw 7-value Stage
3. **[Tier 2]** Department × Source interaction — most department×source cells will be
   single-digit; usable only to spot an outlier worth a follow-up, not to size anything
4. **[Tier 1]** Level (Junior/Mid/Senior, from Job Openings.Level) × Stage funnel — need to
   check level cardinality/counts first, likely 3 buckets over 350 apps is workable
5. **[Tier 2]** Employment Type (Full-time/Part-time/Contract) × Stage funnel — likely
   dominated by one type; check the actual split before assuming this is usable at all
6. **[Tier 2]** Candidate City × Stage funnel — many distinct cities over 300 candidates,
   expect thin cells; only report cities with n≥20
7. **[Tier 1]** Recruiter × Stage funnel + workload-adjusted time-in-stage (only 4
   recruiters, each with 30-113 applications per the earlier People roster — well-powered)
8. **[Tier 1]** Interview Round × Outcome × Recommendation (n=160 interviews, 5 round types
   — workable)

*Candidate segment × offer outcome — all Tier 2, offers n=36 total*
9. Notice Period bucket × Level × Offer-Accept rate — flag explicitly: 36 offers split 3 ways
   will mostly be n<5 per cell; report as directional only, with n shown
10. Expected-vs-Current CTC gap bucket × Accept rate — same n=36 constraint
11. Offer Base CTC vs Salary Band position (below/within/above) × Accept rate — same
    constraint, but worth checking as a possible root cause even at low n
12. Years-experience bucket × Level applied-for — candidate-level (n=300) not offer-level,
    so this one can move to Tier 1 for the mis-leveling question itself, even though its
    downstream link to Accept rate stays Tier 2
13. Candidate City × Offer-Accept rate — Tier 2, n=36 offers across many cities

*Interviewer/quality lens — read together with the department-affinity caveat above; only
6 interviewers, so per-interviewer cuts are Tier 1 on volume but need the affinity caveat*
14. **[Tier 1, caveated]** Interviewer × avg Score × Recommendation mix × downstream Outcome
    (25-33 interviews per interviewer — enough n, but the assignment-affinity finding above
    means "interviewer effect" may be confounded with "which candidates get routed to them,"
    not a clean read on interviewer skill alone)
15. **[Tier 1]** Round × avg Score trend (n=160, 5 rounds — workable, do scores genuinely
    climb Screen→Technical→Bar Raiser or is an early round just noise overridden later?)
16. **[Tier 2]** Same-department vs cross-department interview assignment × avg Score/Outcome
    — the direct test of whether the affinity break above actually matters for quality;
    worth running even at modest n because the answer (matters / doesn't) changes how much
    weight #14 can carry

*Operational timing — Tier 1, application/interview counts support this*
17. Time-in-stage waterfall (Applied→Screened→Interview→Offer→Closed), department-level
    medians *and* the outlier tail — find the real bottleneck instead of assuming one
18. **[Tier 2 — only 24 openings]** Requisition aging: Opened On → Target Close → actual
    Filled date, by department/level; useful as a specific list of overdue reqs even if not
    statistically generalizable
19. Interview scheduling lead time (Applied On → First Interview On) and offer lead time
    (Final Interview On → Offered On), by department/source
20. **[Tier 1, with the right-censoring fix from the correctness re-check applied]** Monthly
    trend of applications, hires, and acceptance rate, excluding the most recent 2-3 months
    to avoid the pipeline-lag bias already found — this is the check for whether the VP's
    "it needs moving" alarm reflects a real trend or a censored recent snapshot

*Referral network — Tier 2, small base (8 candidates) but high-value if a pattern holds*
21. `Referred By` chains — who refers, how many of their referrals convert, is there a
    concentrated set of "super-referrers" worth building a program around (feeds directly
    into candidate E from the current list, with actual evidence behind the sizing, though
    n=8 referral candidates means this is a lead to validate with Acme, not a proof)
22. **[Tier 1]** Rejection Reason × Source × Department, **split by pre-interview vs
    post-interview rejection** (58% of all rejections happen with zero interviews logged —
    this cut needs to separate "never got an interview" from "interviewed and rejected"
    before asking whether Job Board's volume is a real pipeline or mostly resume-stage
    noise; conflating the two would understate how early Job Board applicants actually
    drop off)
23. **[Tier 2, structural output not just a stat]** Candidate/application interview-journey
    table: every application's interviews in order (Round, Outcome, Score, Recommendation)
    alongside the Stage/Status at the time — this is the direct answer to "how many rounds
    did this candidate take and what happened," built once as a reusable view rather than
    answered ad hoc; per the check above it will show mostly 1-2 round journeys with
    non-canonical round ordering, which the output should surface plainly rather than paper
    over
24. **[Tier 1]** No-show/cancellation rate (13.75%, n=160) by Department/Source/Round —
    the magnitude is reportable even though *attribution* (candidate vs company-caused)
    is not recoverable from this schema, as established above; this cut is descriptive
    only and must say so

**Step 2 — challenger pass on every cut, not just a spot-check on the two VP numbers.**
Same discipline that just caught the referral-attribution and Wilson-CI issues above,
applied systematically:
- Recompute the headline number a second, differently-coded way (e.g. pandas groupby vs a
  manual dict aggregation) — must match exactly before it's accepted.
- Every proportion gets a Wilson CI alongside the point estimate, reported together — not
  optional for Tier 1 cuts, and mandatory for any Tier 2 cut that makes it into a deliverable.
- Re-run every source/channel-based cut once on raw candidate identities and once on the
  deduped/canonical view from Step 0, and report the delta — if a conclusion flips between
  the two (like Claim 1's tie did), that conclusion is not usable as-is and gets flagged, not
  quietly resolved in whichever direction is more convenient.
- Any time-based cut gets the right-censoring check applied (exclude or flag the most recent
  2-3 months) before a trend is claimed.
- Any cell with n < 10 gets marked low-confidence explicitly, not silently dropped — "not
  enough data to say" is itself a usable answer and goes in the output.
- One adversarial sentence per surviving finding: "this could be wrong because ___" —
  before it goes in front of anyone.

**Step 3 — how I'd actually build this (once you approve), revised per your instruction to
spend no agent/model bandwidth on the arithmetic itself:** no Agent-tool fan-out for this —
that was more machinery than the problem needs, and it still risks a model summarizing
numbers instead of code computing them. Two plain scripts instead:
- `talentflow/analysis/build_all_views.py` — loads the local JSON once, computes every
  cross-cut in the catalog above (Wilson CIs, dedup-sensitivity, right-censoring exclusion,
  and coarse-bucketing applied as specified per cut) using pandas/stdlib only, and writes
  one CSV per cross-cut plus the interview-journey table to `talentflow/analysis/output/`.
  Fully deterministic, re-runnable, no model call inside it.
- `talentflow/analysis/challenge_all_views.py` — independently recomputes each headline
  number via a different code path (manual dict aggregation instead of pandas groupby, or
  vice versa) and asserts the two agree, printing PASS/FAIL per check. This is the
  "challenger" you asked for, done as code, not as a second model pass eyeballing the first
  one's output — a genuine self-check that fails loudly if something's wrong, in the same
  spirit as a runnable test rather than a review conversation.
- I run both once, read the PASS/FAIL summary and the output CSVs (that's the only place
  this costs conversation turns), and only then write the actual findings into the
  deliverables. Re-running either script later (new data, a challenged number) is free.
- Outputs: one CSV per cross-cut under `talentflow/analysis/output/`, plus a single
  lightweight HTML summary (top-line findings first, then per-cut drill-down tables) in the
  same style as the data browser already published — built for analysis, not raw record
  browsing, and generated from the CSVs, not re-derived by hand.

**Step 4 — only after Steps 1-3 land, revisit the 6-engineer-week list.** The current
A–H candidates are individually real but uniformly small (single-recruiter-week scale). The
correctness re-check already sharpens candidate H (the acceptance-rate dashboard) into
something bigger than "build a metric": it now needs to (i) show every rate with n and a
Wilson CI rather than a bare percentage, and (ii) exclude right-censored recent cohorts from
any trend view by construction — that's a real, non-trivial instrumentation build (M, not S),
and it directly prevents the VP's own team from re-making the mistake this re-check just
caught. Beyond that, once the department/source/level/time cross-cuts are in, I expect more
candidates like this to surface — e.g. if #17 finds one specific stage is the true
department-level bottleneck (not assumed), the fix is a targeted process/tooling change sized
to that evidence, not a generic "add reminders" item; if #14/#16 show real interviewer-
calibration problems (and survive the affinity confound), a scoring/calibration system is a
legitimately bigger (2-3 week) build than anything on the current list. I'm not
pre-committing to specific new candidates here — that's what Steps 1-3 are for — but the list
you saw is a floor, not the ceiling, and I expect it to change.

**Prioritization rule for the final list, so this doesn't drift into over-engineering:**
rank every candidate (old and new) on evidence strength (Tier 1 vs Tier 2, does it survive
the dedup/CI/censoring checks) crossed with effort — take the cheap, well-evidenced fixes
first (A/B/H's core all qualify), but don't pad the remaining budget with three more small
items just to fill 6 weeks if one Tier-1-backed, higher-effort item (the CI-and-censoring
-aware dashboard, or a derived-Stage fix per the schema ledger above) is where the real
leverage actually is. Low-hanging fruit goes first because it's cheap and safe, not because
small is inherently better — the final writeup should say plainly if 2 substantial items
beat 4 small ones.

## What the deep-dive already found

**Claim 1 — "job boards bring 26.9% of hires, biggest channel by a wide margin"**
(Superseded by the correctness re-check above — keeping the original read here for context,
but the deduped/CI-checked version is what goes in D1.) At face value: of 26 `Hired`-stage
applications, 7 trace to Job Board candidates = 26.9%, and Referral also produces exactly 7
hires = 26.9% — a tie. Candidate→hire conversion: Job Board 7/191 = 3.7%, Referral 5/8 =
62.5%, Agency 11.4%, Career Site 16.1%, LinkedIn 9.7%, Campus 0/4. **The tie turned out to be
an artifact of 2 duplicate candidate records spanning both channels** — see the correctness
section for the deduped numbers (Job Board 33.3% of hires once resolved, clearly ahead) and
the confidence intervals (Job Board's low conversion is solid; Referral's exact conversion
rate is not, at n=8). The volume-vs-efficiency framing survives; the precise tie does not.

**Claim 2 — "offer acceptance rate is ~72%"**
36 offers total: 26 Accepted, 5 Declined, 5 Pending. 26/36 = 72.2% (Pending counted as
failure) vs 26/31 = 83.9% (Pending excluded) — an 11.7-point swing on one definitional
choice. **Per the correctness re-check above, the Wilson 95% CIs for these two definitions
overlap ([56.0%,84.2%] vs [67.4%,92.9%])** — at n=36, this isn't a resolvable precision
question, it's a sample-size limitation that D3 needs to design around (report with CI, not
a bare %), on top of the definitional question. Separately: the 5 "Pending" offers are 20 to
**222 days old** (latest data ~2026-08-27) — a 7-month-old "pending" offer is an abandoned
follow-up, not a live decision, which argues for excluding it from "pending" and counting it
as a lapsed non-accept rather than leaving it out of the denominator entirely. Both the
staleness rule and the CI-reporting requirement go into D3.

**Data-quality issues found so far (candidates for D4, with materiality)**
- 6 pairs of candidate records (12 of 300 = 4%) share identical phone + full name but
  different email and Candidate ID — near-certain duplicate people, likely re-applying
  under a different email. This directly risks inflating Job Board's application/
  candidate counts and understating true per-channel conversion (need to re-run Claim 1
  after collapsing these).
- 4 Application IDs (APP-00001, 00005, 00007, 00010) are each reused across two
  completely different application records (different candidates, openings, stages).
  `Application ID` is not a safe join key — anything downstream that joins on it
  instead of the Airtable record `id` silently corrupts.
- All 5 Declined offers still show their linked Application at `Stage = Offer` instead
  of `Rejected` (5/5 — systematic, not noise). `Applications.Stage` lags
  `Offers.Status`; the Offers table is the more trustworthy source for offer outcomes,
  which is itself an input to the D3 metric definition.
- 4 interviews have `Completed On` before `Scheduled On` (temporally impossible).
- 3 offers have `Proposed Start Date` before `Offered On` (temporally impossible).
- Findings table pulled 0 records — expected, it's the write-back table and writes
  403 for us as documented.
- No dangling foreign keys anywhere (Applications→Candidates/Openings, Interviews/
  Offers→Applications, Openings→Departments all clean), no null Source/CTC/experience
  on Candidates, no CTC or negative-experience outliers, no Target-Close-before-Opened
  issues. So the corruption is narrow and specific, not pervasive — matters for how
  hard D4 should hedge.

**Funnel context (for D2 sizing, not yet a verdict)**
- 350 applications → 160 interviews → 36 offers → 26 hires.
- Interview overhead: 10 No Show + 7 Cancelled + 5 Rescheduled = 22/160 (13.8%) of
  scheduled interviews don't complete as planned — a candidate operational-efficiency
  angle independent of both VP claims.
- Job Openings: 11 Open, 8 Filled, 3 On Hold, 2 Cancelled (24 total) — haven't yet
  checked aging on the 11 Open reqs against Target Close.

## Sizing the 6 engineer-weeks (D2 candidate list — first pass, superseded by Step 4 below)

*Note: after reviewing this, the feedback was that these are all roughly one-engineer-week
fixes and the list needs sharper, more ambitious candidates — that's what the "Multi-table
cross-cut plan" section further down (Step 4 specifically) is for. Leaving this first pass
in place as the floor to build on, not the final answer.*

This is the part the plan was missing: a working list of what could actually consume
the 6 weeks, each with a rough size and the evidence behind it, so the eventual "3 to
build / 3 not to build" call in D2 is a ranking of real candidates, not a first draft.
T-shirt sizing: XS ≈ 2-3 days, S ≈ 1 wk, M ≈ 1.5-2 wks, L ≈ 3-4 wks.

| # | Candidate | Size | Evidence from the data | Why it's on the list |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | Auto-sync `Applications.Stage` to `Offers.Status` (Accepted→Hired, Declined→Rejected) | S | 5/5 Declined offers still show Stage=Offer — 100% systematic, not noise | Fixes the pipeline's own bookkeeping; every other number (including the VP's own metric) is downstream of this field being trustworthy |
| B | Stale-offer expiry + recruiter nudge (flag/auto-expire Pending past a decision window) | S | 5 Pending offers aged 20–222 days; a 7-month "pending" offer is an abandoned follow-up, not a live decision | Directly targets what's inflating/obscuring the acceptance-rate number the VP wants moved — closing the loop either recovers real accepts or honestly reclassifies losses |
| C | Candidate de-dup at intake (phone+name match) | M | 6 pairs / 300 candidates (4%) are near-certain duplicates, forked across channels | Protects source attribution long-term; doesn't move either VP number directly, so it's a lower-urgency "hygiene" build unless C's true rate turns out much higher after the dedup re-check in next steps |
| D | Job-board integration as literally requested (deeper ATS/board sync) | L (unscoped — depends which boards/integration type the VP means) | Job Board is highest-volume (236 apps, 191 candidates) but lowest-converting channel (3.7% candidate→hire) — the "wide margin" claim doesn't hold, Referral ties it at the hire level | Likely the VP's literal ask but the data argues against *more volume* being the fix — candidate for "build something different" or explicit not-build, pending the Claim 1 dedup re-check |
| E | Referral program tooling (easier submission + tracking) | S–M | Referral converts 62.5% candidate→hire vs Job Board's 3.7% — the actual wide margin in this data — on only 8 candidates / 13 applications, i.e. under-invested | Best efficiency lever visible in the data; plausible "build something different" answer to the VP's Claim 1 ask instead of literal job-board integration |
| F | Interview no-show/cancellation reduction (reminders/calendar sync) | S | 22/160 scheduled interviews (13.8%) don't complete as planned | Real operational waste, independent of both VP claims — a credible 3rd item if the top ones don't fill 6 weeks |
| G | Open-requisition aging alerts | XS–S (unscoped) | Haven't pulled Target-Close aging on the 11 Open reqs yet — listed in next steps | Placeholder candidate; only keep it if the aging pull turns up something material |
| H | Offer-acceptance-rate dashboard/instrumentation (the actual D3 metric, built) | S | Today the rate only exists as an ad hoc calc off raw exports — no governed metric exists | The VP wants this number tracked and moving; it needs to exist as a real instrumented metric before anyone can "move" it |

**Preliminary read (to be revised once the next-steps checks below are done):** A + B + H
look like the non-negotiable "make the metric trustworthy" foundation (3 weeks combined)
before anything else is worth building on top of it — there's no point optimizing a number
that's currently unreliable by construction. That leaves ~3 weeks for one efficiency bet,
most likely E (referral tooling) over D (literal job-board integration), but that call
depends on the Claim 1 dedup re-check and a rough scope estimate for D — I don't have
enough to size D confidently yet, which itself may be part of the D1 verdict ("can't sign
up to a number for this until it's scoped"). C, F, G are the likely not-build/defer set,
but F could swap in for E if the referral volume turns out too small to matter even after
tooling improves it.
